# enumflags2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/enumflags2/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#enum-flags)Enum Flags

`enumflags2` implements the classic bitflags datastructure. Annotate an enum
with `#[bitflags]`, and `BitFlags<YourEnum>` will be able to hold arbitrary combinations
of your enum within the space of a single integer.

Unlike other crates, `enumflags2` makes the type-level distinction between
a single flag (`YourEnum`) and a set of flags (`BitFlags<YourEnum>`).
This allows idiomatic handling of bitflags, such as with `match` and `iter`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use enumflags2::{bitflags, make_bitflags, BitFlags};
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Test {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C, // unspecified variants pick unused bits automatically
    D = 0b1000,
}
// Flags can be combined with |, this creates a BitFlags of your type:
let a_b: BitFlags<Test> = Test::A | Test::B;
let a_c = Test::A | Test::C;
let b_c_d = make_bitflags!(Test::{B | C | D});
// The debug output lets you inspect both the numeric value and
// the actual flags:
assert_eq!(format!("{:?}", a_b), "BitFlags<Test>(0b11, A | B)");
// But if you'd rather see only one of those, that's available too:
assert_eq!(format!("{}", a_b), "A | B");
assert_eq!(format!("{:04b}", a_b), "0011");
// Iterate over the flags like a normal set
assert_eq!(a_b.iter().collect::<Vec<_>>(), &[Test::A, Test::B]);
// Query the contents with contains and intersects
assert!(a_b.contains(Test::A));
assert!(b_c_d.contains(Test::B | Test::C));
assert!(!(b_c_d.contains(a_b)));
assert!(a_b.intersects(a_c));
assert!(!(a_b.intersects(Test::C | Test::D)));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#optional-feature-flags)Optional Feature Flags

- `serde`- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`for- `BitFlags<T>`.
- `std`implements- `std::error::Error`for- `FromBitsError`.

[§](https://docs.rs#const-fn-compatible-apis)`const fn`-compatible APIs

**Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2632),
which makes it impossible to use any overloaded operators in a const
context.

**Naming convention:** If a separate, more limited function is provided
for usage in a `const fn`, the name is suffixed with `_c`.

Apart from functions whose name ends with `_c`, the [ make_bitflags!](https://docs.rs/macro.make_bitflags.html) macro
is often useful for many

`const` and `const fn` usecases.**Blanket implementations:** If you attempt to write a `const fn` ranging
over `T: BitFlag`, you will be met with an error explaining that currently,
the only allowed trait bound for a `const fn` is `?Sized`. You will probably
want to write a separate implementation for `BitFlags<T, u8>`,
`BitFlags<T, u16>`, etc — best accomplished by a simple macro.

**Documentation considerations:** The strategy described above is often used
by `enumflags2` itself. To avoid clutter in the auto-generated documentation,
the implementations for widths other than `u8` are marked with `#[doc(hidden)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#customizing-default)Customizing `Default`

By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result in an empty
set. If that’s undesirable, you may customize this:

```
#[bitflags(default = B | C)]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Test {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C = 0b0100,
    D = 0b1000,
}
assert_eq!(BitFlags::default(), Test::B | Test::C);
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [make_](https://docs.rs/macro.make_bitflags.html)- bitflags
- `make_bitflags!`provides a succint syntax for creating instances of- `BitFlags<T>`. Instead of repeating the name of your type for each flag you want to add, try- `make_bitflags!(Flags::{Foo | Bar})`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BitFlags](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html)
- Represents a set of flags of some type `T`.`T`must have the`#[bitflags]`attribute applied.
- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstToken.html)- Token
- Workaround for `const fn`limitations.
- [From](https://docs.rs/struct.FromBitsError.html)- Bits - Error
- The error struct used by `BitFlags::from_bits``TryFrom`
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- Iterator that yields each flag set in a `BitFlags`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [BitFlag](https://docs.rs/trait.BitFlag.html)
- A trait automatically implemented by `#[bitflags]`to make the enum a valid type parameter for`BitFlags<T>`.

# enumflags2 0.7.12 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enumflags2/latest

# Enumflags

`enumflags2` implements the classic bitflags datastructure. Annotate an enum
with `#[bitflags]`, and `BitFlags<YourEnum>` will be able to hold arbitrary combinations
of your enum within the space of a single integer.

Unlike other crates, `enumflags2` makes the type-level distinction between
a single flag (`YourEnum`) and a set of flags (`BitFlags<YourEnum>`).
This allows idiomatic handling of bitflags, such as with `match` and `iter`.

## Features

- Uses enums to represent individual flags—a set of flags is a separate type from a single flag.
- Automatically chooses a free bit when you don't specify.
- Detects incorrect BitFlags at compile time.
-  Has a similar API compared to the popular [bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags)crate.
-  Does not expose the generated types explicity. The user interacts exclusively with `struct BitFlags<Enum>;`.
-  The debug formatter prints the binary flag value as well as the flag enums: `BitFlags(0b1111, [A, B, C, D])`.
-  Optional support for serialization with the `serde`

## Example

```
use ;
// Flags can be combined with |, this creates a BitFlags of your type:
let a_b:  = A | B;
let a_c = A | C;
let b_c_d = make_bitflags!;
// The debug output lets you inspect both the numeric value and
// the actual flags:
assert_eq!;
// But if you'd rather see only one of those, that's available too:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over the flags like a normal set
assert_eq!;
// Query the contents with contains and intersects
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
```
## Optional Feature Flags

- `serde`- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`for- `BitFlags<T>`.
- `std`implements- `std::error::Error`for- `FromBitsError`.

`const fn`-compatible APIs

**Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2632),
which makes it impossible to use any overloaded operators in a const
context.

**Naming convention:** If a separate, more limited function is provided
for usage in a `const fn`, the name is suffixed with `_c`.

Apart from functions whose name ends with `_c`, the [`make_bitflags!`] macro
is often useful for many `const` and `const fn` usecases.

**Blanket implementations:** If you attempt to write a `const fn` ranging
over `T: BitFlag`, you will be met with an error explaining that currently,
the only allowed trait bound for a `const fn` is `?Sized`. You will probably
want to write a separate implementation for `BitFlags<T, u8>`,
`BitFlags<T, u16>`, etc — best accomplished by a simple macro.

**Documentation considerations:** The strategy described above is often used
by `enumflags2` itself. To avoid clutter in the auto-generated documentation,
the implementations for widths other than `u8` are marked with `#[doc(hidden)]`.

## Customizing `Default`

By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result in an empty
set. If that's undesirable, you may customize this:

```
assert_eq!;
```

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

assert!(a_b.contains(Test::A));
assert!(b_c_d.contains(Test::B | Test::C));
assert!(!(b_c_d.contains(a_b)));
assert!(a_b.intersects(a_c));
assert!(!(a_b.intersects(Test::C | Test::D)));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#optional-feature-flags)Optional Feature Flags

- `serde`- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`for- `BitFlags<T>`.
- `std`implements- `std::error::Error`for- `FromBitsError`.

[§](https://docs.rs#const-fn-compatible-apis)`const fn`-compatible APIs

**Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2632),
which makes it impossible to use any overloaded operators in a const
context.

**Naming convention:** If a separate, more limited function is provided
for usage in a `const fn`, the name is suffixed with `_c`.

Apart from functions whose name ends with `_c`, the [ make_bitflags!](https://docs.rs/macro.make_bitflags.html) macro
is often useful for many

`const` and `const fn` usecases.**Blanket implementations:** If you attempt to write a `const fn` ranging
over `T: BitFlag`, you will be met with an error explaining that currently,
the only allowed trait bound for a `const fn` is `?Sized`. You will probably
want to write a separate implementation for `BitFlags<T, u8>`,
`BitFlags<T, u16>`, etc — best accomplished by a simple macro.

**Documentation considerations:** The strategy described above is often used
by `enumflags2` itself. To avoid clutter in the auto-generated documentation,
the implementations for widths other than `u8` are marked with `#[doc(hidden)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#customizing-default)Customizing `Default`

By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result in an empty
set. If that’s undesirable, you may customize this:

```
#[bitflags(default = B | C)]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Test {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C = 0b0100,
    D = 0b1000,
}
assert_eq!(BitFlags::default(), Test::B | Test::C);
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [make_](https://docs.rs/macro.make_bitflags.html)- bitflags
- `make_bitflags!`provides a succint syntax for creating instances of- `BitFlags<T>`. Instead of repeating the name of your type for each flag you want to add, try- `make_bitflags!(Flags::{Foo | Bar})`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BitFlags](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html)
- Represents a set of flags of some type `T`.`T`must have the`#[bitflags]`attribute applied.
- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstToken.html)- Token
- Workaround for `const fn`limitations.
- [From](https://docs.rs/struct.FromBitsError.html)- Bits - Error
- The error struct used by `BitFlags::from_bits``TryFrom`
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- Iterator that yields each flag set in a `BitFlags`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [BitFlag](https://docs.rs/trait.BitFlag.html)
- A trait automatically implemented by `#[bitflags]`to make the enum a valid type parameter for`BitFlags<T>`.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# sim_lib_numbers_tensor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-numbers-tensor/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_numbers_tensor/

## Expand description

The n-dimensional tensor number domain: the uniform `Tensor` value, its
domain registration and constructors (`tensor`, `vec`, `mat`, …), and the
`SpecTensor` interface that specialized element-type backends plug into.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [domains](https://docs.rs/domains/index.html)
- Canonical symbols for the number-domain family.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Spec](https://docs.rs/struct.SpecTensorDescriptor.html)- Tensor - Descriptor
- Metadata describing one registered `SpecTensor`backend, surfaced as a descriptor value so the registry can advertise the specialized tensor.
- [Tensor](https://docs.rs/struct.Tensor.html)
- The uniform tensor value: an n-dimensional array of scalar number cells.
- [Tensor](https://docs.rs/struct.TensorNumbersLib.html)- Numbers - Lib
- Registered number-domain library that installs the `numbers/tensor`domain.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Spec](https://docs.rs/trait.SpecTensor.html)- Tensor
- Interface a specialized element-type tensor backend implements to bridge its
own storage and the uniform `Tensor`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_scalar_tensor_value.html)- scalar_ - tensor_ - value
- Builds a rank-0 scalar tensor wrapping a single scalar number `value`.
- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_tensor_value.html)- tensor_ - value
- Builds a tensor `Value``shape`from row-major`data`cells.
- [checked_](https://docs.rs/fn.checked_element_count.html)- element_ - count
- The number of cells in a tensor of the given shape, failing closed when the
dimension product overflows `usize`instead of wrapping (release) or panicking (debug).
- [element_](https://docs.rs/fn.element_count.html)- count
- The number of cells in a tensor of the given shape. An empty shape is a
scalar (one cell). This is the one home for the `element_count`helper that the generic, broadcast, linalg, and every typed tensor crate re-grew.
- [flatten_](https://docs.rs/fn.flatten_tensor_scalar_cells.html)- tensor_ - scalar_ - cells
- Clones a tensor’s row-major cell values as a flat vector.
- [number_](https://docs.rs/fn.number_domain.html)- domain

- [number_](https://docs.rs/fn.number_literal_for_tensor_cell.html)- literal_ - for_ - tensor_ - cell
- Extracts the canonical `NumberLiteral``value`, or`None`if the value is not a number. Shared backing for the typed literal-cell parsers below.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_complex_literal_cell.html)- complex_ - literal_ - cell

- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_f64_literal_cell.html)- f64_ - literal_ - cell

- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_i64_literal_cell.html)- i64_ - literal_ - cell
- Parses a tensor cell as an `i64`, returning`None`unless it is a number in the`numbers/i64`domain whose canonical form parses cleanly.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_rational_literal_cell.html)- rational_ - literal_ - cell
- Parses a tensor cell as a `(numerator, denominator)`rational pair, returning`None`unless it is a number in the`numbers/rational`domain whose canonical`num/den`form parses cleanly.
- [spec_](https://docs.rs/fn.spec_tensor_descriptor_value.html)- tensor_ - descriptor_ - value
- Encodes a `SpecTensorDescriptor``kind`,`symbol`,`dtype`,`implementation`, and`storage`entries.
- [spec_](https://docs.rs/fn.spec_tensor_symbol.html)- tensor_ - symbol
- Builds a descriptor symbol (`numbers/tensor-spec/<name>`) for a specialized tensor backend.
- [tensor_](https://docs.rs/fn.tensor_dtype.html)- dtype

- [tensor_](https://docs.rs/fn.tensor_value_class_symbol.html)- value_ - class_ - symbol

- [tensor_](https://docs.rs/fn.tensor_value_ref.html)- value_ - ref

# kglite_mcp_server - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kglite-mcp-server/0.12.10/kglite_mcp_server/

## Expand description

`kglite-mcp-server` — single MCP server for KGLite knowledge graphs.

Layers three kglite-specific tools on top of the generic
`mcp-server` framework: `cypher_query`, `graph_overview`, and
`save_graph`. All three close over a [`GraphState`] holding the
active `KnowledgeGraph` Python object.

[§](https://docs.rs#two-frontends-one-library)Two frontends, one library

The server body lives in [ run](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html) (sync, builds its own tokio
runtime) so it can be driven from two places without duplication:

- the thin `src/main.rs`binary (`cargo install kglite-mcp-server`), which is libpython-free; and
- the `kglite`Python wheel, whose PyO3 wrapper calls`run``py.detach(...)`(GIL released) so`pip install kglite`ships the exact same server with no separate wheel and no duplicated engine.

The library never links libpython — it depends only on the pure-Rust
`kglite` core. The wheel’s `.so` and the standalone binary share this
one engine build.

Modes:

- `--graph X.kgl`— load a pre-built graph file at boot.
- `--workspace DIR`— multi-repo. Post-activate hook runs- `kglite.code_tree.build()`on each cloned repo.
- `--watch DIR`— file-watcher mode. Change handler rebuilds the code-tree graph and atomic-swaps the active slot.
- `--source-root DIR`— generic file-tree mode (no graph).
- bare — framework + manifest tools only.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [run](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html)
- Run the MCP server to completion over stdio.
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_with_embedder_factory.html)- with_ - embedder_ - factory
- Like `run``extensions.embedder.library`Python path (`sentence-transformers`/`fastembed`). The standalone binary calls`run`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [PyEmbedder](https://docs.rs/type.PyEmbedderFactory.html)- Factory
- Builds a graph embedder from the manifest’s `extensions.embedder`config (passed as a JSON string), on demand.

## Expand description

hiker — a tiny DSL for stating architectural intent.

Pipeline (one module per compiler stage; build them in this order):
lexer   : &str        -> Vec

The front end (lexer/parser/checker) is language-agnostic; only the chosen backend is target-specific.

# pseudoroot

A Rust implementation of fakeroot using library interposition
(`LD_PRELOAD` on Linux, `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` on macOS). Commands run as
if they had root privileges without requiring real root access.

## Quick start

```
# Implicit run (fakeroot-style)
# Explicit subcommand form (equivalent)
```
`pdr` is a single self-contained binary — the interposed library is embedded
at build time and extracted to a cache directory on first use, so no
`libpseudoroot_lib.so`/`.dylib` needs to exist anywhere on disk beforehand.
`pdr start` runs the optional persistent daemon in-process, so no separate
`pdrd` binary is needed for that either; a standalone `pdrd` is still
available (see [Build and test](https://docs.rs#build-and-test)) as a dedicated daemon
process for external orchestration.

## CLI options

| Option | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--uid <UID>` | Fake UID | 0 |
| `--gid <GID>` | Fake GID | 0 |
| `--daemon` | Attach to an existing `pdrd`instead of a per-invocation session | off |
| `--socket-path <PATH>` | Daemon socket path | `/tmp/pseudoroot.sock` |
| `start`/`stop`/`status` | Manage the daemon | — |
| `print-library-path` | Print the interposed library path | — |
| `start --verbose` | Enable verbose daemon logging | off |
| `start --cleanup` | Clean up socket file on daemon exit | off |

By default each invocation gets its own session, shared across `exec`
within it. To share state across separate invocations, use a daemon:

```
```
## Rust API (fakeroost-compatible)

Swap backends by changing the import only:

```
use FakerootCommandExt;
```
## Environment variables

- `PSEUDOROOT_UID`/- `PSEUDOROOT_GID`— fake uid/gid (default: 0)
- `PSEUDOROOT_DAEMON_SOCKET`— attach to an existing daemon (skips session auto-start)
- `PSEUDOROOT_STANDALONE`— per-process state only (no session)
- `PSEUDOROOT_SESSION_SHM`— set to- `0`to use an in-process daemon thread instead of the shared-memory map for session mode
- `PSEUDOROOT_LIB`— override the interposed library path, bypassing the embedded copy entirely (tests, custom installs, debugging a locally built- `pseudoroot-lib`)

## Documentation

- [Architecture](https://docs.rs/docs/architecture.md)— crate layout, inode-keyed state model, platform support, interposed syscall families.
- [Benchmarks](https://docs.rs/docs/benchmarks.md)— comparison against native,- `fakeroot`, and- `fakeroost`; on a 128-core Linux machine pseudoroot sustains ~7.4M faked- `stat()`calls/sec vs fakeroot's ~44.5K, and on a MacBook Pro with M2 Max (12-core ARM64) ~899K calls/sec vs fakeroot's ~43K.

## Comparison

| Feature | pseudoroot | fakeroot | fakeroost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | `LD_PRELOAD` | `LD_PRELOAD` | ptrace supervisor |
| Platforms | Linux, macOS | Linux | Linux |
| xattr / setcap | Faked | Faked | Faked |
| mknod unprivileged | Placeholder + fake metadata | Yes | Yes |
| Multi-process state | SHM session or daemon ( `pdrd`) | `faked` | N/A (single run) |
| Rust API | `FakerootCommandExt` | C only | `FakerootCommandExt` |

## Build and test

```
```
`pdr` embeds the interposed library at build time: `pseudoroot/build.rs`
compiles the cdylib from the source bundled at `pseudoroot/interpose/` and
`include_bytes!`es it into the binary — so `cargo install pseudoroot` from
crates.io is self-contained, with no separate `.so`/`.dylib` to install.
For a standalone `pdrd` daemon binary, build the `pseudoroot-daemon` package
directly: `cargo build -p pseudoroot-daemon`.

# RustDiff

Semantic JSON, XML & SQL diff tool with a native GTK4 + Libadwaita desktop UI.

Language: **English** | [Espanol](https://docs.rs/README.es.md)

## Features

- Semantic JSON, XML & SQL diff (objects, arrays, XML nodes, attributes, text, and SQL statements)

- Side-by-side editors with syntax highlighting
- **Busqueda en editores**(- `Ctrl+F`) con navegacion siguiente/anterior y wrap-around
- Auto compare while typing (debounced) + manual compare
- Difference table with filters and click-to-jump navigation
- Export to `.txt`and styled`.html`

# mmio_rs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mmio-rs/0.2.0/mmio_rs/

## Expand description

Zero-overhead, `no_std` memory-mapped I/O register abstraction.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use mmio_rs::prelude::*;
// Implement a critical section for your target once per binary.
mmio_rs::impl_critical_section!(
    acquire: { /* disable interrupts, return previous state */ 0 },
    release: |_state| { /* restore interrupt state */ }
);
// Define a peripheral's register layout.
mmio_rs::register_block! {
    pub struct Uart @ 0x4000_1000 {
        dr:  u32 => ReadWrite @ 0x00,
        sr:  u32 => ReadOnly  @ 0x04,
        brr: u32 => ReadWrite @ 0x08,
    }
}
// Use it.
Uart::dr().write(b'A' as u32);
let status = Uart::sr().read();
Uart::brr().write_field(0xFFFF, 0, 0x0683); // set baud divisor
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Convenience re-export of the most commonly used types.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_critical_section.html)- critical_ - section
- Implement this macro once in your project to provide the critical section.
- [register_](https://docs.rs/macro.register_block.html)- block
- Define a register block with named fields and a static base address.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Atomic](https://docs.rs/struct.AtomicRegister.html)- Register
- Wraps a `Register``critical_section`
- [Dynamic](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamicRegisterBlock.html)- Register - Block
- Like `RegisterBlock``T`and access marker`Access`are fixed at construction time, and the base address can be set after creation.
- [IrqGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.IrqGuard.html)
- RAII guard that acquires the critical section on creation and releases it on drop.
- [Read](https://docs.rs/struct.ReadOnly.html)- Only
- Access marker: register can only be read.
- [Read](https://docs.rs/struct.ReadWrite.html)- Write
- Access marker: register can be both read and written.
- [Register](https://docs.rs/struct.Register.html)
- A typed pointer to a single memory-mapped register.
- [Register](https://docs.rs/struct.RegisterBlock.html)- Block
- A fixed-size array of `N`registers sharing a base address, addressed by index.
- [Write](https://docs.rs/struct.WriteOnly.html)- Only
- Access marker: register can only be written.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [critical_](https://docs.rs/fn.critical_section.html)- section
- Executes `f`inside a critical section, returning its result.

# kglite-bolt-server 0.12.10 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/kglite-bolt-server/0.12.10

# kglite-bolt-server

**Bolt v5.x protocol server for  kglite
knowledge graphs.** A pure-Rust single binary speaking the Neo4j
wire protocol — the Neo4j driver ecosystem (Python / JS / Java /
Go / .NET drivers, Cypher Shell, Neo4j Browser, BloodHound,
LangChain's

`Neo4jGraph`) plugs in unchanged.```
```
Then point any Neo4j-aware client at `bolt://localhost:7687` and
run Cypher against the loaded `.kgl` graph.

## Features (Phase F)

- **Bolt v5.x handshake + PackStream framing**(handshake versions 5.0 / 5.1 / 5.2 / 5.3 / 5.4 advertised).
- `neo4j://`routing URIs- `--advertise-addr`for reverse-proxy deployments).
- **TLS**via- `--tls-cert`+- `--tls-key`(drivers connect with- `bolt+s://`or- `neo4j+s://`).
- `db.labels()`/- `db.relationshipTypes()`- `label`,- `relationshipType`).
- **Optimistic concurrency control**on commit — concurrent writers whose snapshots become stale see- `Neo.ClientError.Transaction.ConflictDetected`. Retry on the client side.
- **Zero PyO3 in the binary**— no libpython link, no Python runtime required.- `cargo tree -p kglite-bolt-server | grep pyo3`returns empty.

## CLI

```
kglite-bolt-server [OPTIONS] --graph <PATH>
Options:
  --graph <PATH>               .kgl graph file to serve
  --bind <ADDR>                Bind address [default: 127.0.0.1]
  --port <PORT>                Port [default: 7687]
  --readonly                   Reject mutations
  --auth <USER:PASS>           Basic auth credentials
  --idle-timeout <SECS>        Per-session idle timeout
  --max-sessions <N>           Max concurrent sessions
  --advertise-addr <HOST:PORT> Address advertised in routing table (for neo4j:// URIs)
  --tls-cert <PATH>            PEM-encoded TLS certificate chain
  --tls-key <PATH>             PEM-encoded TLS private key
```
## Documentation

- [Bolt server operator guide](https://kglite.readthedocs.io/en/latest/operators/bolt-server.html)
- [kglite Rust API](https://docs.rs/kglite)

MIT — see [LICENSE](https://github.com/kkollsga/kglite/blob/main/LICENSE).

# pseudoroot_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pseudoroot-core/0.2.0/pseudoroot_core/

## Expand description

Core types and state management for pseudoroot

This crate provides the shared data structures and state management for the pseudoroot library interposition system.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use state::`- [FakeInode](https://docs.rs/state/struct.FakeInode.html);
- `pub use state::`- [FakeRootState](https://docs.rs/state/struct.FakeRootState.html);
- `pub use state::`- [InodeKey](https://docs.rs/state/type.InodeKey.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [daemon_](https://docs.rs/daemon_client/index.html)- client
- Daemon client for connecting to pseudoroot-daemon
- [daemon_](https://docs.rs/daemon_server/index.html)- server
- In-process and standalone fake-root daemon server.
- [protocol](https://docs.rs/protocol/index.html)
- IPC protocol for communication between pseudoroot-lib and pseudoroot-daemon
- [shm_](https://docs.rs/shm_client/index.html)- client
- Client-side access to an inherited session shared-memory map.
- [shm_map](https://docs.rs/shm_map/index.html)
- Experimental shared-memory inode map for session mode (Linux and macOS).

# snowbridge_pallet_outbound_queue - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/snowbridge-pallet-outbound-queue/0.23.0/snowbridge_pallet_outbound_queue/

## Expand description

Pallet for committing outbound messages for delivery to Ethereum

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

Messages come either from sibling parachains via XCM, or BridgeHub itself
via the `snowbridge-pallet-system`:

- `snowbridge_outbound_queue_primitives::v1::EthereumBlobExporter::deliver`
- `snowbridge_pallet_system::Pallet::send`

The message submission pipeline works like this:

- The message is first validated via the implementation for
`snowbridge_outbound_queue_primitives::v1::SendMessage::validate`
- The message is then enqueued for later processing via the implementation for
`snowbridge_outbound_queue_primitives::v1::SendMessage::deliver`
- The underlying message queue is implemented by `Config::MessageQueue`
- The message queue delivers messages back to this pallet via the implementation for
`frame_support::traits::ProcessMessage::process_message`
- The message is processed in `Pallet::do_process_message`: a. Assigned a nonce b. ABI-encoded, hashed, and stored in the`MessageLeaves`vector
- At the end of the block, a merkle root is constructed from all the leaves in `MessageLeaves`.
- This merkle root is inserted into the parachain header as a digest item
- Offchain relayers are able to relay the message to Ethereum after: a. Generating a merkle
proof for the committed message using the `prove_message`runtime API b. Reading the actual message content from the`Messages`vector in storage

On the Ethereum side, the message root is ultimately the thing being verified by the Polkadot light client.

[§](https://docs.rs#message-priorities)Message Priorities

The processing of governance commands can never be halted. This effectively allows us to pause processing of normal user messages while still allowing governance commands to be sent to Ethereum.

[§](https://docs.rs#fees)Fees

An upfront fee must be paid for delivering a message. This fee covers several components:

- The weight of processing the message locally
- The gas refund paid out to relayers for message submission
- An additional reward paid out to relayers for message submission

Messages are weighed to determine the maximum amount of gas they could consume on Ethereum. Using this upper bound, a final fee can be calculated.

The fee calculation also requires the following parameters:

- Average ETH/DOT exchange rate over some period
- Max fee per unit of gas that bridge is willing to refund relayers for

By design, it is expected that governance should manually update these
parameters every few weeks using the `set_pricing_parameters` extrinsic in the
system pallet.

This is an interim measure. Once ETH/DOT liquidity pools are available in the Polkadot network, we’ll use them as a source of pricing info, subject to certain safeguards.

[§](https://docs.rs#fee-computation-function)Fee Computation Function

```
LocalFee(Message) = WeightToFee(ProcessMessageWeight(Message))
RemoteFee(Message) = MaxGasRequired(Message) * Params.MaxFeePerGas + Params.Reward
RemoteFeeAdjusted(Message) = Params.Multiplier * (RemoteFee(Message) / Params.Ratio("ETH/DOT"))
Fee(Message) = LocalFee(Message) + RemoteFeeAdjusted(Message)
```
By design, the computed fee includes a safety factor (the `Multiplier`) to cover
unfavourable fluctuations in the ETH/DOT exchange rate.

[§](https://docs.rs#fee-settlement)Fee Settlement

On the remote side, in the gateway contract, the relayer accrues

`Min(GasPrice, Message.MaxFeePerGas) * GasUsed() + Message.Reward`Or in plain english, relayers are refunded for gas consumption, using a
price that is a minimum of the actual gas price, or `Message.MaxFeePerGas`.

[§](https://docs.rs#extrinsics)Extrinsics

- `Call::set_operating_mode`

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-api)Runtime API

- `prove_message`: Generate a merkle proof for a committed message
- `calculate_fee`: Calculate the delivery fee for a message

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use types::`- [ProcessMessageOriginOf](https://docs.rs/types/type.ProcessMessageOriginOf.html);
- `pub use weights::`- [WeightInfo](https://docs.rs/weights/trait.WeightInfo.html);
- `pub use`- [pallet](https://docs.rs/pallet/index.html)::*;

- [process_](https://docs.rs/process_message_impl/index.html)- message_ - impl

# enumflags2 0.7.12 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enumflags2/0.7.12

# Enumflags

`enumflags2` implements the classic bitflags datastructure. Annotate an enum
with `#[bitflags]`, and `BitFlags<YourEnum>` will be able to hold arbitrary combinations
of your enum within the space of a single integer.

Unlike other crates, `enumflags2` makes the type-level distinction between
a single flag (`YourEnum`) and a set of flags (`BitFlags<YourEnum>`).
This allows idiomatic handling of bitflags, such as with `match` and `iter`.

## Features

- Uses enums to represent individual flags—a set of flags is a separate type from a single flag.
- Automatically chooses a free bit when you don't specify.
- Detects incorrect BitFlags at compile time.
-  Has a similar API compared to the popular [bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags)crate.
-  Does not expose the generated types explicity. The user interacts exclusively with `struct BitFlags<Enum>;`.
-  The debug formatter prints the binary flag value as well as the flag enums: `BitFlags(0b1111, [A, B, C, D])`.
-  Optional support for serialization with the `serde`

## Example

```
use ;
// Flags can be combined with |, this creates a BitFlags of your type:
let a_b:  = A | B;
let a_c = A | C;
let b_c_d = make_bitflags!;
// The debug output lets you inspect both the numeric value and
// the actual flags:
assert_eq!;
// But if you'd rather see only one of those, that's available too:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over the flags like a normal set
assert_eq!;
// Query the contents with contains and intersects
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
```
## Optional Feature Flags

- `serde`- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`for- `BitFlags<T>`.
- `std`implements- `std::error::Error`for- `FromBitsError`.

`const fn`-compatible APIs

**Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2632),
which makes it impossible to use any overloaded operators in a const
context.

**Naming convention:** If a separate, more limited function is provided
for usage in a `const fn`, the name is suffixed with `_c`.

Apart from functions whose name ends with `_c`, the [`make_bitflags!`] macro
is often useful for many `const` and `const fn` usecases.

**Blanket implementations:** If you attempt to write a `const fn` ranging
over `T: BitFlag`, you will be met with an error explaining that currently,
the only allowed trait bound for a `const fn` is `?Sized`. You will probably
want to write a separate implementation for `BitFlags<T, u8>`,
`BitFlags<T, u16>`, etc — best accomplished by a simple macro.

**Documentation considerations:** The strategy described above is often used
by `enumflags2` itself. To avoid clutter in the auto-generated documentation,
the implementations for widths other than `u8` are marked with `#[doc(hidden)]`.

## Customizing `Default`

By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result in an empty
set. If that's undesirable, you may customize this:

```
assert_eq!;
```

# enumflags2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enumflags2/0.7.12/target-redirect/enumflags2/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#enum-flags)Enum Flags

`enumflags2` implements the classic bitflags datastructure. Annotate an enum
with `#[bitflags]`, and `BitFlags<YourEnum>` will be able to hold arbitrary combinations
of your enum within the space of a single integer.

Unlike other crates, `enumflags2` makes the type-level distinction between
a single flag (`YourEnum`) and a set of flags (`BitFlags<YourEnum>`).
This allows idiomatic handling of bitflags, such as with `match` and `iter`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use enumflags2::{bitflags, make_bitflags, BitFlags};
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Test {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C, // unspecified variants pick unused bits automatically
    D = 0b1000,
}
// Flags can be combined with |, this creates a BitFlags of your type:
let a_b: BitFlags<Test> = Test::A | Test::B;
let a_c = Test::A | Test::C;
let b_c_d = make_bitflags!(Test::{B | C | D});
// The debug output lets you inspect both the numeric value and
// the actual flags:
assert_eq!(format!("{:?}", a_b), "BitFlags<Test>(0b11, A | B)");
// But if you'd rather see only one of those, that's available too:
assert_eq!(format!("{}", a_b), "A | B");
assert_eq!(format!("{:04b}", a_b), "0011");
// Iterate over the flags like a normal set
assert_eq!(a_b.iter().collect::<Vec<_>>(), &[Test::A, Test::B]);
// Query the contents with contains and intersects
assert!(a_b.contains(Test::A));
assert!(b_c_d.contains(Test::B | Test::C));
assert!(!(b_c_d.contains(a_b)));
assert!(a_b.intersects(a_c));
assert!(!(a_b.intersects(Test::C | Test::D)));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#optional-feature-flags)Optional Feature Flags

- `serde`- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`for- `BitFlags<T>`.
- `std`implements- `std::error::Error`for- `FromBitsError`.

[§](https://docs.rs#const-fn-compatible-apis)`const fn`-compatible APIs

**Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2632),
which makes it impossible to use any overloaded operators in a const
context.

**Naming convention:** If a separate, more limited function is provided
for usage in a `const fn`, the name is suffixed with `_c`.

Apart from functions whose name ends with `_c`, the [ make_bitflags!](https://docs.rs/macro.make_bitflags.html) macro
is often useful for many

`const` and `const fn` usecases.**Blanket implementations:** If you attempt to write a `const fn` ranging
over `T: BitFlag`, you will be met with an error explaining that currently,
the only allowed trait bound for a `const fn` is `?Sized`. You will probably
want to write a separate implementation for `BitFlags<T, u8>`,
`BitFlags<T, u16>`, etc — best accomplished by a simple macro.

**Documentation considerations:** The strategy described above is often used
by `enumflags2` itself. To avoid clutter in the auto-generated documentation,
the implementations for widths other than `u8` are marked with `#[doc(hidden)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#customizing-default)Customizing `Default`

By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result in an empty
set. If that’s undesirable, you may customize this:

```
#[bitflags(default = B | C)]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Test {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C = 0b0100,
    D = 0b1000,
}
assert_eq!(BitFlags::default(), Test::B | Test::C);
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [make_](https://docs.rs/macro.make_bitflags.html)- bitflags
- `make_bitflags!`provides a succint syntax for creating instances of- `BitFlags<T>`. Instead of repeating the name of your type for each flag you want to add, try- `make_bitflags!(Flags::{Foo | Bar})`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BitFlags](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html)
- Represents a set of flags of some type `T`.`T`must have the`#[bitflags]`attribute applied.
- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstToken.html)- Token
- Workaround for `const fn`limitations.
- [From](https://docs.rs/struct.FromBitsError.html)- Bits - Error
- The error struct used by `BitFlags::from_bits``TryFrom`
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- Iterator that yields each flag set in a `BitFlags`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [BitFlag](https://docs.rs/trait.BitFlag.html)
- A trait automatically implemented by `#[bitflags]`to make the enum a valid type parameter for`BitFlags<T>`.

[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! // Query the contents with contains and intersects
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! assert!(a_b.contains(Test::A));
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! assert!(b_c_d.contains(Test::B | Test::C));
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! assert!(!(b_c_d.contains(a_b)));
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! assert!(a_b.intersects(a_c));
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! assert!(!(a_b.intersects(Test::C | Test::D)));
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! ```
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! ## Optional Feature Flags
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! - [`serde`](https://serde.rs/) implements `Serialize` and `Deserialize`
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!   for `BitFlags<T>`.
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! - `std` implements `std::error::Error` for `FromBitsError`.
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! ## `const fn`-compatible APIs
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! **Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage][const-trait-rfc],
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! which makes it impossible to use any overloaded operators in a const
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! context.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! **Naming convention:** If a separate, more limited function is provided
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! for usage in a `const fn`, the name is suffixed with `_c`.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! Apart from functions whose name ends with `_c`, the [`make_bitflags!`] macro
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! is often useful for many `const` and `const fn` usecases.
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! **Blanket implementations:** If you attempt to write a `const fn` ranging
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! over `T: BitFlag`, you will be met with an error explaining that currently,
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! the only allowed trait bound for a `const fn` is `?Sized`. You will probably
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! want to write a separate implementation for `BitFlags<T, u8>`,
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! `BitFlags<T, u16>`, etc — best accomplished by a simple macro.
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! **Documentation considerations:** The strategy described above is often used
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! by `enumflags2` itself. To avoid clutter in the auto-generated documentation,
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! the implementations for widths other than `u8` are marked with `#[doc(hidden)]`.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! ## Customizing `Default`
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result in an empty
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! set. If that's undesirable, you may customize this:
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! ```
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! # use enumflags2::{BitFlags, bitflags};
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! #[bitflags(default = B | C)]
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! #[repr(u8)]
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! enum Test {
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!     A = 0b0001,
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!     B = 0b0010,
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!     C = 0b0100,
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!     D = 0b1000,
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! }
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! assert_eq!(BitFlags::default(), Test::B | Test::C);
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! ```
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//!
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! [const-trait-rfc]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2632
[99](https://docs.rs#99)#![warn(missing_docs)]
[100](https://docs.rs#100)#![cfg_attr(all(not(test), not(feature = "std")), no_std)]

[114](https://docs.rs#114)macro_rules! for_each_uint {
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    ( $d:tt $tyvar:ident $dd:tt $docattr:ident => $($input:tt)* ) => {
[116](https://docs.rs#116)        macro_rules! implement {
[117](https://docs.rs#117)            ( $d $tyvar:ty => $d($d $docattr:meta)? ) => {
[118](https://docs.rs#118)                $($input)*
[119](https://docs.rs#119)            }
[120](https://docs.rs#120)        }
[121](https://docs.rs#121)
[122](https://docs.rs#122)        implement! { u8 => }
[123](https://docs.rs#123)        implement! { u16 => doc(hidden) }
[124](https://docs.rs#124)        implement! { u32 => doc(hidden) }
[125](https://docs.rs#125)        implement! { u64 => doc(hidden) }
[126](https://docs.rs#126)        implement! { u128 => doc(hidden) }
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    }

[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// A trait automatically implemented by `#[bitflags]` to make the enum
[131](https://docs.rs#131)/// a valid type parameter for `BitFlags<T>`.
[132](https://docs.rs#132)pub trait BitFlag: Copy + Clone + 'static + _internal::RawBitFlags {
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    /// Create a `BitFlags` with no flags set (in other words, with a value of 0).
[134](https://docs.rs#134)    ///
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    /// This is a convenience reexport of [`BitFlags::empty`]. It can be called with
[136](https://docs.rs#136)    /// `MyFlag::empty()`, thus bypassing the need for type hints in some situations.
[137](https://docs.rs#137)    ///
[138](https://docs.rs#138)    /// ```
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    /// #[bitflags]
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[142](https://docs.rs#142)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    /// enum MyFlag {
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[145](https://docs.rs#145)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    /// }
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    ///
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    /// use enumflags2::BitFlag;
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    ///
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    /// let empty = MyFlag::empty();
[152](https://docs.rs#152)    /// assert!(empty.is_empty());
[153](https://docs.rs#153)    /// assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::One), false);
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    /// assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::Two), false);
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    /// assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    /// ```
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    #[inline]
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    fn empty() -> BitFlags<Self> {
[159](https://docs.rs#159)        BitFlags::empty()
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    }
[161](https://docs.rs#161)
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    /// Create a `BitFlags` with all flags set.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    ///
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    /// This is a convenience reexport of [`BitFlags::all`]. It can be called with
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    /// `MyFlag::all()`, thus bypassing the need for type hints in some situations.
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    ///
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    /// ```
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    /// #[bitflags]
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// enum MyFlag {
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// }
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    ///
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    /// use enumflags2::BitFlag;
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    ///
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// let all = MyFlag::all();
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    /// assert!(all.is_all());
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    /// assert_eq!(all.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    /// assert_eq!(all.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    /// assert_eq!(all.contains(MyFlag::Three), true);
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    /// ```
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    #[inline]
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    fn all() -> BitFlags<Self> {
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        BitFlags::all()
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    }
[190](https://docs.rs#190)
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    /// Create a `BitFlags` if the raw value provided does not contain
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    /// any illegal flags.
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    ///
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    /// This is a convenience reexport of [`BitFlags::from_bits`]. It can be called
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    /// with `MyFlag::from_bits(bits)`, thus bypassing the need for type hints in
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    /// some situations.
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    ///
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    /// ```
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    /// #[bitflags]
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    /// enum MyFlag {
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    /// }
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    ///
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    /// use enumflags2::BitFlag;
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    ///
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    /// let flags = MyFlag::from_bits(0b11).unwrap();
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    /// let invalid = MyFlag::from_bits(1 << 3);
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    /// assert!(invalid.is_err());
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    /// ```
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    #[inline]
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    fn from_bits(bits: Self::Numeric) -> Result<BitFlags<Self>, FromBitsError<Self>> {
[220](https://docs.rs#220)        BitFlags::from_bits(bits)
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    }
[222](https://docs.rs#222)
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    /// Create a `BitFlags` from an underlying bitwise value. If any
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// invalid bits are set, ignore them.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    ///
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    /// This is a convenience reexport of [`BitFlags::from_bits_truncate`]. It can be
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    /// called with `MyFlag::from_bits_truncate(bits)`, thus bypassing the need for
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// type hints in some situations.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    ///
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    /// ```
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// #[bitflags]
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    /// enum MyFlag {
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    /// }
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    ///
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// use enumflags2::BitFlag;
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    ///
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    /// let flags = MyFlag::from_bits_truncate(0b1_1011);
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    /// ```
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    #[inline]
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    fn from_bits_truncate(bits: Self::Numeric) -> BitFlags<Self> {
[250](https://docs.rs#250)        BitFlags::from_bits_truncate(bits)
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    }
[252](https://docs.rs#252)
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    /// Create a `BitFlags` unsafely, without checking if the bits form
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    /// a valid bit pattern for the type.
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    ///
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    /// Consider using [`from_bits`][BitFlag::from_bits]
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// or [`from_bits_truncate`][BitFlag::from_bits_truncate] instead.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    /// # Safety
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    ///
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// All bits set in `val` must correspond to a value of the enum.
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    ///
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    /// # Example
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    ///
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    /// This is a convenience reexport of [`BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked`]. It can be
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    /// called with `MyFlag::from_bits_unchecked(bits)`, thus bypassing the need for
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// type hints in some situations.
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    ///
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// ```
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    /// #[bitflags]
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// enum MyFlag {
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    /// }
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    ///
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    /// use enumflags2::BitFlag;
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    ///
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    /// let flags = unsafe {
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    ///     MyFlag::from_bits_unchecked(0b011)
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    /// };
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    ///
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    /// ```
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    #[inline]
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    unsafe fn from_bits_unchecked(bits: Self::Numeric) -> BitFlags<Self> {
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked(bits)
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    }

[296](https://docs.rs#296)/// While the module is public, this is only the case because it needs to be

[301](https://docs.rs#301)    /// A trait automatically implemented by `#[bitflags]` to make the enum
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    /// a valid type parameter for `BitFlags<T>`.
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    ///
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    /// # Safety
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    ///
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    /// The values should reflect reality, like they do if the implementation
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    /// is generated by the procmacro.
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    ///
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    /// `bits` must return the same value as
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    /// [`transmute_copy`][std::mem::transmute_copy].
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    ///
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    /// Representations for all values of `T` must have exactly one bit set.
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    pub unsafe trait RawBitFlags: Copy + Clone + 'static {
[314](https://docs.rs#314)        /// The underlying integer type.
[315](https://docs.rs#315)        type Numeric: BitFlagNum;
[316](https://docs.rs#316)
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        /// A value with no bits set.
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        const EMPTY: Self::Numeric;
[319](https://docs.rs#319)
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        /// The value used by the Default implementation. Equivalent to EMPTY, unless
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        /// customized.
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        const DEFAULT: Self::Numeric;
[323](https://docs.rs#323)
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        /// A value with all flag bits set.
[325](https://docs.rs#325)        const ALL_BITS: Self::Numeric;
[326](https://docs.rs#326)
[327](https://docs.rs#327)        /// The name of the type for debug formatting purposes.
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        ///
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        /// This is typically `BitFlags<EnumName>`
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        const BITFLAGS_TYPE_NAME: &'static str;
[331](https://docs.rs#331)
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        /// Return the bits as a number type.
[333](https://docs.rs#333)        fn bits(self) -> Self::Numeric;
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    }
