[425](https://docs.rs#425)
[426](https://docs.rs#426)/// Represents a set of flags of some type `T`.
[427](https://docs.rs#427)/// `T` must have the `#[bitflags]` attribute applied.
[428](https://docs.rs#428)///
[429](https://docs.rs#429)/// A `BitFlags<T>` is as large as the `T` itself,
[430](https://docs.rs#430)/// and stores one flag per bit.
[431](https://docs.rs#431)///
[432](https://docs.rs#432)/// ## Comparison operators, [`PartialOrd`] and [`Ord`]
[433](https://docs.rs#433)///
[434](https://docs.rs#434)/// To make it possible to use `BitFlags` as the key of a
[435](https://docs.rs#435)/// [`BTreeMap`][std::collections::BTreeMap], `BitFlags` implements
[436](https://docs.rs#436)/// [`Ord`]. There is no meaningful total order for bitflags,
[437](https://docs.rs#437)/// so the implementation simply compares the integer values of the bits.
[438](https://docs.rs#438)///
[439](https://docs.rs#439)/// Unfortunately, this means that comparing `BitFlags` with an operator
[440](https://docs.rs#440)/// like `<=` will compile, and return values that are probably useless
[441](https://docs.rs#441)/// and not what you expect. In particular, `<=` does *not* check whether
[442](https://docs.rs#442)/// one value is a subset of the other. Use [`BitFlags::contains`] for that.
[443](https://docs.rs#443)///
[444](https://docs.rs#444)/// ## Customizing `Default`
[445](https://docs.rs#445)///
[446](https://docs.rs#446)/// By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result
[447](https://docs.rs#447)/// in an empty set. If that's undesirable, you may customize this:
[448](https://docs.rs#448)///
[449](https://docs.rs#449)/// ```
[450](https://docs.rs#450)/// # use enumflags2::{BitFlags, bitflags};
[451](https://docs.rs#451)/// #[bitflags(default = B | C)]
[452](https://docs.rs#452)/// #[repr(u8)]
[453](https://docs.rs#453)/// #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
[454](https://docs.rs#454)/// enum MyFlag {
[455](https://docs.rs#455)///     A = 0b0001,
[456](https://docs.rs#456)///     B = 0b0010,
[457](https://docs.rs#457)///     C = 0b0100,
[458](https://docs.rs#458)///     D = 0b1000,
[459](https://docs.rs#459)/// }
[460](https://docs.rs#460)///
[461](https://docs.rs#461)/// assert_eq!(BitFlags::default(), MyFlag::B | MyFlag::C);
[462](https://docs.rs#462)/// ```
[463](https://docs.rs#463)///
[464](https://docs.rs#464)/// ## Memory layout
[465](https://docs.rs#465)///
[466](https://docs.rs#466)/// `BitFlags<T>` is marked with the `#[repr(transparent)]` trait, meaning
[467](https://docs.rs#467)/// it can be safely transmuted into the corresponding numeric type.
[468](https://docs.rs#468)///
[469](https://docs.rs#469)/// Usually, the same can be achieved by using [`BitFlags::bits`] in one
[470](https://docs.rs#470)/// direction, and [`BitFlags::from_bits`], [`BitFlags::from_bits_truncate`],
[471](https://docs.rs#471)/// or [`BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked`] in the other direction. However,
[472](https://docs.rs#472)/// transmuting might still be useful if, for example, you're dealing with
[473](https://docs.rs#473)/// an entire array of `BitFlags`.
[474](https://docs.rs#474)///
[475](https://docs.rs#475)/// When transmuting *into* a `BitFlags`, make sure that each set bit
[476](https://docs.rs#476)/// corresponds to an existing flag
[477](https://docs.rs#477)/// (cf. [`from_bits_unchecked`][BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked]).
[478](https://docs.rs#478)///
[479](https://docs.rs#479)/// For example:
[480](https://docs.rs#480)///
[481](https://docs.rs#481)/// ```
[482](https://docs.rs#482)/// # use enumflags2::{BitFlags, bitflags};
[483](https://docs.rs#483)/// #[bitflags]
[484](https://docs.rs#484)/// #[repr(u8)] // <-- the repr determines the numeric type
[485](https://docs.rs#485)/// #[derive(Copy, Clone)]
[486](https://docs.rs#486)/// enum TransmuteMe {
[487](https://docs.rs#487)///     One = 1 << 0,
[488](https://docs.rs#488)///     Two = 1 << 1,
[489](https://docs.rs#489)/// }
[490](https://docs.rs#490)///
[491](https://docs.rs#491)/// # use std::slice;
[492](https://docs.rs#492)/// // NOTE: we use a small, self-contained function to handle the slice
[493](https://docs.rs#493)/// // conversion to make sure the lifetimes are right.
[494](https://docs.rs#494)/// fn transmute_slice<'a>(input: &'a [BitFlags<TransmuteMe>]) -> &'a [u8] {
[495](https://docs.rs#495)///     unsafe {
[496](https://docs.rs#496)///         slice::from_raw_parts(input.as_ptr() as *const u8, input.len())
[497](https://docs.rs#497)///     }
[498](https://docs.rs#498)/// }
[499](https://docs.rs#499)///
[500](https://docs.rs#500)/// let many_flags = &[
[501](https://docs.rs#501)///     TransmuteMe::One.into(),
[502](https://docs.rs#502)///     TransmuteMe::One | TransmuteMe::Two,
[503](https://docs.rs#503)/// ];
[504](https://docs.rs#504)///
[505](https://docs.rs#505)/// let as_nums = transmute_slice(many_flags);
[506](https://docs.rs#506)/// assert_eq!(as_nums, &[0b01, 0b11]);
[507](https://docs.rs#507)/// ```
[508](https://docs.rs#508)///
[509](https://docs.rs#509)/// ## Implementation notes
[510](https://docs.rs#510)///
[511](https://docs.rs#511)/// You might expect this struct to be defined as
[512](https://docs.rs#512)///
[513](https://docs.rs#513)/// ```ignore
[514](https://docs.rs#514)/// struct BitFlags<T: BitFlag> {
[515](https://docs.rs#515)///     value: T::Numeric
[516](https://docs.rs#516)/// }
[517](https://docs.rs#517)/// ```
[518](https://docs.rs#518)///
[519](https://docs.rs#519)/// Ideally, that would be the case. However, because `const fn`s cannot
[520](https://docs.rs#520)/// have trait bounds in current Rust, this would prevent us from providing
[521](https://docs.rs#521)/// most `const fn` APIs. As a workaround, we define `BitFlags` with two
[522](https://docs.rs#522)/// type parameters, with a default for the second one:
[523](https://docs.rs#523)///
[524](https://docs.rs#524)/// ```ignore
[525](https://docs.rs#525)/// struct BitFlags<T, N = <T as BitFlag>::Numeric> {
[526](https://docs.rs#526)///     value: N,
[527](https://docs.rs#527)///     marker: PhantomData<T>,
[528](https://docs.rs#528)/// }
[529](https://docs.rs#529)/// ```
[530](https://docs.rs#530)///
[531](https://docs.rs#531)/// Manually providing a type for the `N` type parameter shouldn't ever
[532](https://docs.rs#532)/// be necessary.
[533](https://docs.rs#533)///
[534](https://docs.rs#534)/// The types substituted for `T` and `N` must always match, creating a
[535](https://docs.rs#535)/// `BitFlags` value where that isn't the case is only possible with
[536](https://docs.rs#536)/// incorrect unsafe code.
[537](https://docs.rs#537)#[derive(Copy, Clone)]
[538](https://docs.rs#538)#[repr(transparent)]
[539](https://docs.rs#539)pub struct BitFlags<T, N = <T as _internal::RawBitFlags>::Numeric> {
[540](https://docs.rs#540)    val: N,
[541](https://docs.rs#541)    marker: PhantomData<T>,
[542](https://docs.rs#542)}
[543](https://docs.rs#543)
[544](https://docs.rs#544)/// `make_bitflags!` provides a succint syntax for creating instances of
[545](https://docs.rs#545)/// `BitFlags<T>`. Instead of repeating the name of your type for each flag
[546](https://docs.rs#546)/// you want to add, try `make_bitflags!(Flags::{Foo | Bar})`.
[547](https://docs.rs#547)/// ```
[548](https://docs.rs#548)/// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags, make_bitflags};
[549](https://docs.rs#549)/// # #[bitflags]
[550](https://docs.rs#550)/// # #[repr(u8)]
[551](https://docs.rs#551)/// # #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
[552](https://docs.rs#552)/// # enum Test {
[553](https://docs.rs#553)/// #     A = 1 << 0,
[554](https://docs.rs#554)/// #     B = 1 << 1,
[555](https://docs.rs#555)/// #     C = 1 << 2,
[556](https://docs.rs#556)/// # }
[557](https://docs.rs#557)/// let x = make_bitflags!(Test::{A | C});
[558](https://docs.rs#558)/// assert_eq!(x, Test::A | Test::C);
[559](https://docs.rs#559)///
[560](https://docs.rs#560)/// // Also works in const contexts:
[561](https://docs.rs#561)/// const X: BitFlags<Test> = make_bitflags!(Test::A);
[562](https://docs.rs#562)/// ```
[563](https://docs.rs#563)#[macro_export]
[564](https://docs.rs#564)macro_rules! make_bitflags {
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    ( $enum:ident ::{ $($variant:ident)|* } ) => {
[566](https://docs.rs#566)        {
[567](https://docs.rs#567)            let mut n = 0;
[568](https://docs.rs#568)            $(
[569](https://docs.rs#569)                {
[570](https://docs.rs#570)                    let flag: $enum = $enum::$variant;
[571](https://docs.rs#571)                    n |= flag as <$enum as $crate::_internal::RawBitFlags>::Numeric;
[572](https://docs.rs#572)                }
[573](https://docs.rs#573)            )*
[574](https://docs.rs#574)            // SAFETY: The value has been created from numeric values of the underlying
[575](https://docs.rs#575)            // enum, so only valid bits are set.
[576](https://docs.rs#576)            unsafe { $crate::BitFlags::<$enum>::from_bits_unchecked_c(
[577](https://docs.rs#577)                    n, $crate::BitFlags::CONST_TOKEN) }
[578](https://docs.rs#578)        }
[579](https://docs.rs#579)    };
[580](https://docs.rs#580)    ( $enum:ident :: $variant:ident ) => {
[581](https://docs.rs#581)        {
[582](https://docs.rs#582)            let flag: $enum = $enum::$variant;
[583](https://docs.rs#583)            let n = flag as <$enum as $crate::_internal::RawBitFlags>::Numeric;
[584](https://docs.rs#584)            // SAFETY: The value has been created from the numeric value of
[585](https://docs.rs#585)            // the underlying enum, so only valid bits are set.
[586](https://docs.rs#586)            unsafe { $crate::BitFlags::<$enum>::from_bits_unchecked_c(
[587](https://docs.rs#587)                    n, $crate::BitFlags::CONST_TOKEN) }
[588](https://docs.rs#588)        }
[589](https://docs.rs#589)    };
[590](https://docs.rs#590)}
[591](https://docs.rs#591)

[593](https://docs.rs#593)/// unless [customized](index.html#customizing-default).
[594](https://docs.rs#594)impl<T> Default for BitFlags<T>

[602](https://docs.rs#602)            marker: PhantomData,
[603](https://docs.rs#603)        }
[604](https://docs.rs#604)    }

[613](https://docs.rs#613)
[614](https://docs.rs#614)impl<T> BitFlags<T>
[615](https://docs.rs#615)where
[616](https://docs.rs#616)    T: BitFlag,
[617](https://docs.rs#617){
[618](https://docs.rs#618)    /// Create a `BitFlags` if the raw value provided does not contain
[619](https://docs.rs#619)    /// any illegal flags.
[620](https://docs.rs#620)    ///
[621](https://docs.rs#621)    /// See also: [a convenience re-export in the `BitFlag` trait][BitFlag::from_bits],
[622](https://docs.rs#622)    /// which can help avoid the need for type hints.
[623](https://docs.rs#623)    ///
[624](https://docs.rs#624)    /// ```
[625](https://docs.rs#625)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[626](https://docs.rs#626)    /// #[bitflags]
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[628](https://docs.rs#628)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
[629](https://docs.rs#629)    /// enum MyFlag {
[630](https://docs.rs#630)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[631](https://docs.rs#631)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[632](https://docs.rs#632)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[633](https://docs.rs#633)    /// }
[634](https://docs.rs#634)    ///
[635](https://docs.rs#635)    /// let flags: BitFlags<MyFlag> = BitFlags::from_bits(0b11).unwrap();
[636](https://docs.rs#636)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[637](https://docs.rs#637)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[638](https://docs.rs#638)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    /// let invalid = BitFlags::<MyFlag>::from_bits(1 << 3);
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    /// assert!(invalid.is_err());
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    /// ```
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    #[inline]
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    pub fn from_bits(bits: T::Numeric) -> Result<Self, FromBitsError<T>> {
[644](https://docs.rs#644)        let flags = Self::from_bits_truncate(bits);
[645](https://docs.rs#645)        if flags.bits() == bits {
[646](https://docs.rs#646)            Ok(flags)
[647](https://docs.rs#647)        } else {
[648](https://docs.rs#648)            Err(FromBitsError {
[649](https://docs.rs#649)                flags,
[650](https://docs.rs#650)                invalid: bits & !flags.bits(),
[651](https://docs.rs#651)            })
[652](https://docs.rs#652)        }
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    }
[654](https://docs.rs#654)
[655](https://docs.rs#655)    /// Create a `BitFlags` from an underlying bitwise value. If any
[656](https://docs.rs#656)    /// invalid bits are set, ignore them.
[657](https://docs.rs#657)    ///
[658](https://docs.rs#658)    /// See also: [a convenience re-export in the `BitFlag` trait][BitFlag::from_bits_truncate],
[659](https://docs.rs#659)    /// which can help avoid the need for type hints.
[660](https://docs.rs#660)    ///
[661](https://docs.rs#661)    /// ```
[662](https://docs.rs#662)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[663](https://docs.rs#663)    /// #[bitflags]
[664](https://docs.rs#664)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[665](https://docs.rs#665)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[666](https://docs.rs#666)    /// enum MyFlag {
[667](https://docs.rs#667)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[668](https://docs.rs#668)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[669](https://docs.rs#669)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[670](https://docs.rs#670)    /// }
[671](https://docs.rs#671)    ///
[672](https://docs.rs#672)    /// let flags: BitFlags<MyFlag> = BitFlags::from_bits_truncate(0b1_1011);
[673](https://docs.rs#673)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[674](https://docs.rs#674)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[675](https://docs.rs#675)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[676](https://docs.rs#676)    /// ```
[677](https://docs.rs#677)    #[must_use]
[678](https://docs.rs#678)    #[inline(always)]
[679](https://docs.rs#679)    pub fn from_bits_truncate(bits: T::Numeric) -> Self {
[680](https://docs.rs#680)        // SAFETY: We're truncating out all the invalid bits, so the remaining
[681](https://docs.rs#681)        // ones must be valid.
[682](https://docs.rs#682)        unsafe { BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked(bits & T::ALL_BITS) }
[683](https://docs.rs#683)    }
[684](https://docs.rs#684)
[685](https://docs.rs#685)    /// Create a new BitFlags unsafely, without checking if the bits form
[686](https://docs.rs#686)    /// a valid bit pattern for the type.
[687](https://docs.rs#687)    ///
[688](https://docs.rs#688)    /// Consider using [`from_bits`][BitFlags::from_bits]
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    /// or [`from_bits_truncate`][BitFlags::from_bits_truncate] instead.
[690](https://docs.rs#690)    ///
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    /// # Safety
[692](https://docs.rs#692)    ///
[693](https://docs.rs#693)    /// All bits set in `val` must correspond to a value of the enum.
[694](https://docs.rs#694)    ///
[695](https://docs.rs#695)    /// # Example
[696](https://docs.rs#696)    ///
[697](https://docs.rs#697)    /// ```
[698](https://docs.rs#698)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[699](https://docs.rs#699)    /// #[bitflags]
[700](https://docs.rs#700)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[701](https://docs.rs#701)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[702](https://docs.rs#702)    /// enum MyFlag {
[703](https://docs.rs#703)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[704](https://docs.rs#704)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[705](https://docs.rs#705)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[706](https://docs.rs#706)    /// }
[707](https://docs.rs#707)    ///
[708](https://docs.rs#708)    /// let flags: BitFlags<MyFlag> = unsafe {
[709](https://docs.rs#709)    ///     BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked(0b011)
[710](https://docs.rs#710)    /// };
[711](https://docs.rs#711)    ///
[712](https://docs.rs#712)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[713](https://docs.rs#713)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[714](https://docs.rs#714)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[715](https://docs.rs#715)    /// ```
[716](https://docs.rs#716)    #[must_use]
[717](https://docs.rs#717)    #[inline(always)]
[718](https://docs.rs#718)    pub unsafe fn from_bits_unchecked(val: T::Numeric) -> Self {
[719](https://docs.rs#719)        BitFlags {
[720](https://docs.rs#720)            val,
[721](https://docs.rs#721)            marker: PhantomData,
[722](https://docs.rs#722)        }
[723](https://docs.rs#723)    }
[724](https://docs.rs#724)
[725](https://docs.rs#725)    /// Turn a `T` into a `BitFlags<T>`. Also available as `flag.into()`.
[726](https://docs.rs#726)    #[must_use]
[727](https://docs.rs#727)    #[inline(always)]
[728](https://docs.rs#728)    pub fn from_flag(flag: T) -> Self {
[729](https://docs.rs#729)        // SAFETY: A value of the underlying enum is valid by definition.
[730](https://docs.rs#730)        unsafe { Self::from_bits_unchecked(flag.bits()) }
[731](https://docs.rs#731)    }
[732](https://docs.rs#732)
[733](https://docs.rs#733)    /// Create a `BitFlags` with no flags set (in other words, with a value of `0`).
[734](https://docs.rs#734)    ///
[735](https://docs.rs#735)    /// See also: [`BitFlag::empty`], a convenience reexport;
[736](https://docs.rs#736)    /// [`BitFlags::EMPTY`], the same functionality available
[737](https://docs.rs#737)    /// as a constant for `const fn` code.
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    ///
[739](https://docs.rs#739)    /// ```
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[741](https://docs.rs#741)    /// #[bitflags]
[742](https://docs.rs#742)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[743](https://docs.rs#743)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    /// enum MyFlag {
[745](https://docs.rs#745)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[746](https://docs.rs#746)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[747](https://docs.rs#747)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[748](https://docs.rs#748)    /// }
[749](https://docs.rs#749)    ///
[750](https://docs.rs#750)    /// let empty: BitFlags<MyFlag> = BitFlags::empty();
[751](https://docs.rs#751)    /// assert!(empty.is_empty());
[752](https://docs.rs#752)    /// assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::One), false);
[753](https://docs.rs#753)    /// assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::Two), false);
[754](https://docs.rs#754)    /// assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[755](https://docs.rs#755)    /// ```
[756](https://docs.rs#756)    #[inline(always)]
[757](https://docs.rs#757)    pub fn empty() -> Self {
[758](https://docs.rs#758)        Self::EMPTY
[759](https://docs.rs#759)    }
[760](https://docs.rs#760)
[761](https://docs.rs#761)    /// Create a `BitFlags` with all flags set.
[762](https://docs.rs#762)    ///
[763](https://docs.rs#763)    /// See also: [`BitFlag::all`], a convenience reexport;
[764](https://docs.rs#764)    /// [`BitFlags::ALL`], the same functionality available
[765](https://docs.rs#765)    /// as a constant for `const fn` code.
[766](https://docs.rs#766)    ///
[767](https://docs.rs#767)    /// ```
[768](https://docs.rs#768)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[769](https://docs.rs#769)    /// #[bitflags]
[770](https://docs.rs#770)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[771](https://docs.rs#771)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[772](https://docs.rs#772)    /// enum MyFlag {
[773](https://docs.rs#773)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[774](https://docs.rs#774)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[775](https://docs.rs#775)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,

# make_bitflags in enumflags2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/enumflags2/0.7.12/enumflags2/macro.make_bitflags.html

```
macro_rules! make_bitflags {
    ( $enum:ident ::{ $($variant:ident)|* } ) => { ... };
    ( $enum:ident :: $variant:ident ) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

`make_bitflags!` provides a succint syntax for creating instances of
`BitFlags<T>`. Instead of repeating the name of your type for each flag
you want to add, try `make_bitflags!(Flags::{Foo | Bar})`.

```
let x = make_bitflags!(Test::{A | C});
assert_eq!(x, Test::A | Test::C);
// Also works in const contexts:
const X: BitFlags<Test> = make_bitflags!(Test::A);
```

---

# BitFlags in enumflags2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/enumflags2/0.7.12/enumflags2/struct.BitFlags.html

`pub struct BitFlags<T, N = <T as RawBitFlags>::Numeric> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Represents a set of flags of some type `T`.
`T` must have the `#[bitflags]` attribute applied.

A `BitFlags<T>` is as large as the `T` itself,
and stores one flag per bit.

[§](https://docs.rs#comparison-operators-partialord-and-ord)Comparison operators, `PartialOrd``Ord`

`PartialOrd``Ord`To make it possible to use `BitFlags` as the key of a
[`BTreeMap`][std::collections::BTreeMap], `BitFlags` implements
[ Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html). There is no meaningful total order for bitflags,
so the implementation simply compares the integer values of the bits.

Unfortunately, this means that comparing `BitFlags` with an operator
like `<=` will compile, and return values that are probably useless
and not what you expect. In particular, `<=` does *not* check whether
one value is a subset of the other. Use [ BitFlags::contains](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.contains) for that.

[§](https://docs.rs#customizing-default)Customizing `Default`

By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result
in an empty set. If that’s undesirable, you may customize this:

```
#[bitflags(default = B | C)]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum MyFlag {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C = 0b0100,
    D = 0b1000,
}
assert_eq!(BitFlags::default(), MyFlag::B | MyFlag::C);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#memory-layout)Memory layout

`BitFlags<T>` is marked with the `#[repr(transparent)]` trait, meaning
it can be safely transmuted into the corresponding numeric type.

Usually, the same can be achieved by using [ BitFlags::bits](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.bits) in one
direction, and

[,](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits)

`BitFlags::from_bits`[, or](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits_truncate)

`BitFlags::from_bits_truncate`[in the other direction. However, transmuting might still be useful if, for example, you’re dealing with an entire array of](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits_unchecked)

`BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked``BitFlags`.When transmuting *into* a `BitFlags`, make sure that each set bit
corresponds to an existing flag
(cf. [ from_bits_unchecked](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits_unchecked)).

For example:

```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)] // <-- the repr determines the numeric type
#[derive(Copy, Clone)]
enum TransmuteMe {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
}
// NOTE: we use a small, self-contained function to handle the slice
// conversion to make sure the lifetimes are right.
fn transmute_slice<'a>(input: &'a [BitFlags<TransmuteMe>]) -> &'a [u8] {
    unsafe {
        slice::from_raw_parts(input.as_ptr() as *const u8, input.len())
    }
}
let many_flags = &[
    TransmuteMe::One.into(),
    TransmuteMe::One | TransmuteMe::Two,
];
let as_nums = transmute_slice(many_flags);
assert_eq!(as_nums, &[0b01, 0b11]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-notes)Implementation notes

You might expect this struct to be defined as

Ideally, that would be the case. However, because `const fn`s cannot
have trait bounds in current Rust, this would prevent us from providing
most `const fn` APIs. As a workaround, we define `BitFlags` with two
type parameters, with a default for the second one:

Manually providing a type for the `N` type parameter shouldn’t ever
be necessary.

The types substituted for `T` and `N` must always match, creating a
`BitFlags` value where that isn’t the case is only possible with
incorrect unsafe code.

Create a `BitFlags<T>` from an underlying bitwise value. If any
invalid bits are set, ignore them.

```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
const FLAGS: BitFlags<MyFlag> =
    BitFlags::<MyFlag>::from_bits_truncate_c(0b10101010, BitFlags::CONST_TOKEN);
assert_eq!(FLAGS, MyFlag::Two);
```
Bitwise OR — return value contains flag if either argument does.

Also available as `a | b`, but operator overloads are not usable
in `const fn`s at the moment.

Bitwise NOT — return value contains flag if argument doesn’t.

Also available as `!a`, but operator overloads are not usable
in `const fn`s at the moment.

Moreover, due to `const fn` limitations, `not_c` needs a
[ ConstToken](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstToken.html) as an argument.

```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
const FLAGS: BitFlags<MyFlag> = make_bitflags!(MyFlag::{One | Two});
const NEGATED: BitFlags<MyFlag> = FLAGS.not_c(BitFlags::CONST_TOKEN);
assert_eq!(NEGATED, MyFlag::Three);
```

Create a `BitFlags` if the raw value provided does not contain
any illegal flags.

See also: [a convenience re-export in the  BitFlag trait](https://docs.rs/trait.BitFlag.html#method.from_bits),
which can help avoid the need for type hints.

```
#[bitflags]

enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
let flags: BitFlags<MyFlag> = BitFlags::from_bits(0b11).unwrap();
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);

```

Create a new BitFlags unsafely, without checking if the bits form a valid bit pattern for the type.

`from_bits_truncate`[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

All bits set in `val` must correspond to a value of the enum.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
let flags: BitFlags<MyFlag> = unsafe {
    BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked(0b011)
};
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
```
Create a `BitFlags` with no flags set (in other words, with a value of `0`).

See also: [ BitFlag::empty](https://docs.rs/trait.BitFlag.html#method.empty), a convenience reexport;

[, the same functionality available as a constant for](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#associatedconstant.EMPTY)

`BitFlags::EMPTY``const fn` code.```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
let empty: BitFlags<MyFlag> = BitFlags::empty();
assert!(empty.is_empty());
assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::One), false);
assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::Two), false);

```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/enumflags2/lib.rs.html#843-845)

#### pub fn [intersects](https://docs.rs#method.intersects)<B: [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[BitFlags](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html)<T>>>(self, other: B) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html)

Returns true if at least one flag is shared.

Returns true if all flags are contained.

Inserts if `cond` holds, else removes

```
#[bitflags]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Debug)]
#[repr(u8)]
enum MyFlag {
    A = 1 << 0,
    B = 1 << 1,
    C = 1 << 2,
}
let mut state = MyFlag::A | MyFlag::C;
state.set(MyFlag::A | MyFlag::B, false);
// Because the condition was false, both
// `A` and `B` are removed from the set
assert_eq!(state, MyFlag::C);
```

# ConstToken in enumflags2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/enumflags2/0.7.12/enumflags2/struct.ConstToken.html

`pub struct ConstToken<T, N>(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

Workaround for `const fn` limitations.

Some `const fn`s in this crate will need an instance of this type
for some type-level information usually provided by traits.

A token can be obtained from [ BitFlags::CONST_TOKEN](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#associatedconstant.CONST_TOKEN). The relevant types
should be readily inferred from context.

For an example of usage, see [ not_c](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.not_c).

# FromBitsError in enumflags2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/enumflags2/0.7.12/enumflags2/struct.FromBitsError.html

`pub struct FromBitsError<T: `[BitFlag](https://docs.rs/trait.BitFlag.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

The error struct used by [ BitFlags::from_bits](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits)
and the

[implementation for invalid values.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.TryFrom.html)

`TryFrom`Note that the implementation of [`std::error::Error`]
for this type is gated on the `std` feature flag.

```
#[bitflags]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
#[repr(u8)]
enum MyFlags {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C = 0b0100,
    D = 0b1000,
}
let result: Result<BitFlags<MyFlags>, _> = 0b10101u8.try_into();
assert!(result.is_err());
let error = result.unwrap_err();
assert_eq!(error.truncate(), MyFlags::C | MyFlags::A);
assert_eq!(error.invalid_bits(), 0b10000);
```

A trait automatically implemented by `#[bitflags]` to make the enum
a valid type parameter for `BitFlags<T>`.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Create a `BitFlags` with no flags set (in other words, with a value of 0).

This is a convenience reexport of [ BitFlags::empty](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.empty). It can be called with

`MyFlag::empty()`, thus bypassing the need for type hints in some situations.```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
use enumflags2::BitFlag;
let empty = MyFlag::empty();
assert!(empty.is_empty());
assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::One), false);
assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::Two), false);
assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
```
Create a `BitFlags` with all flags set.

This is a convenience reexport of [ BitFlags::all](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.all). It can be called with

`MyFlag::all()`, thus bypassing the need for type hints in some situations.```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
use enumflags2::BitFlag;
let all = MyFlag::all();
assert!(all.is_all());
assert_eq!(all.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
assert_eq!(all.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
assert_eq!(all.contains(MyFlag::Three), true);
```

Create a `BitFlags` if the raw value provided does not contain
any illegal flags.

This is a convenience reexport of [ BitFlags::from_bits](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits). It can be called

some situations.```

# enumflags2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/enumflags2/latest/enumflags2/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#enum-flags)Enum Flags

`enumflags2` implements the classic bitflags datastructure. Annotate an enum
with `#[bitflags]`, and `BitFlags<YourEnum>` will be able to hold arbitrary combinations
of your enum within the space of a single integer.

Unlike other crates, `enumflags2` makes the type-level distinction between
a single flag (`YourEnum`) and a set of flags (`BitFlags<YourEnum>`).
This allows idiomatic handling of bitflags, such as with `match` and `iter`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use enumflags2::{bitflags, make_bitflags, BitFlags};
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Test {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C, // unspecified variants pick unused bits automatically
    D = 0b1000,
}
// Flags can be combined with |, this creates a BitFlags of your type:
let a_b: BitFlags<Test> = Test::A | Test::B;
let a_c = Test::A | Test::C;
let b_c_d = make_bitflags!(Test::{B | C | D});
// The debug output lets you inspect both the numeric value and
// the actual flags:
assert_eq!(format!("{:?}", a_b), "BitFlags<Test>(0b11, A | B)");
// But if you'd rather see only one of those, that's available too:
assert_eq!(format!("{}", a_b), "A | B");
assert_eq!(format!("{:04b}", a_b), "0011");
// Iterate over the flags like a normal set
assert_eq!(a_b.iter().collect::<Vec<_>>(), &[Test::A, Test::B]);
// Query the contents with contains and intersects
assert!(a_b.contains(Test::A));
assert!(b_c_d.contains(Test::B | Test::C));
assert!(!(b_c_d.contains(a_b)));
assert!(a_b.intersects(a_c));
assert!(!(a_b.intersects(Test::C | Test::D)));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#optional-feature-flags)Optional Feature Flags

- `serde`- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`for- `BitFlags<T>`.
- `std`implements- `std::error::Error`for- `FromBitsError`.

[§](https://docs.rs#const-fn-compatible-apis)`const fn`-compatible APIs

**Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2632),
which makes it impossible to use any overloaded operators in a const
context.

**Naming convention:** If a separate, more limited function is provided
for usage in a `const fn`, the name is suffixed with `_c`.

Apart from functions whose name ends with `_c`, the [ make_bitflags!](https://docs.rs/macro.make_bitflags.html) macro
is often useful for many

`const` and `const fn` usecases.**Blanket implementations:** If you attempt to write a `const fn` ranging
over `T: BitFlag`, you will be met with an error explaining that currently,
the only allowed trait bound for a `const fn` is `?Sized`. You will probably
want to write a separate implementation for `BitFlags<T, u8>`,
`BitFlags<T, u16>`, etc — best accomplished by a simple macro.

**Documentation considerations:** The strategy described above is often used
by `enumflags2` itself. To avoid clutter in the auto-generated documentation,
the implementations for widths other than `u8` are marked with `#[doc(hidden)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#customizing-default)Customizing `Default`

By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result in an empty
set. If that’s undesirable, you may customize this:

```
#[bitflags(default = B | C)]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Test {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C = 0b0100,
    D = 0b1000,
}
assert_eq!(BitFlags::default(), Test::B | Test::C);
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [make_](https://docs.rs/macro.make_bitflags.html)- bitflags
- `make_bitflags!`provides a succint syntax for creating instances of- `BitFlags<T>`. Instead of repeating the name of your type for each flag you want to add, try- `make_bitflags!(Flags::{Foo | Bar})`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BitFlags](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html)
- Represents a set of flags of some type `T`.`T`must have the`#[bitflags]`attribute applied.
- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstToken.html)- Token
- Workaround for `const fn`limitations.
- [From](https://docs.rs/struct.FromBitsError.html)- Bits - Error
- The error struct used by `BitFlags::from_bits``TryFrom`
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- Iterator that yields each flag set in a `BitFlags`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [BitFlag](https://docs.rs/trait.BitFlag.html)
- A trait automatically implemented by `#[bitflags]`to make the enum a valid type parameter for`BitFlags<T>`.

# enumflags2 0.7.11 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enumflags2/0.7.11

# Enumflags

`enumflags2` implements the classic bitflags datastructure. Annotate an enum
with `#[bitflags]`, and `BitFlags<YourEnum>` will be able to hold arbitrary combinations
of your enum within the space of a single integer.

Unlike other crates, `enumflags2` makes the type-level distinction between
a single flag (`YourEnum`) and a set of flags (`BitFlags<YourEnum>`).
This allows idiomatic handling of bitflags, such as with `match` and `iter`.

## Features

- Uses enums to represent individual flags—a set of flags is a separate type from a single flag.
- Automatically chooses a free bit when you don't specify.
- Detects incorrect BitFlags at compile time.
-  Has a similar API compared to the popular [bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags)crate.
-  Does not expose the generated types explicity. The user interacts exclusively with `struct BitFlags<Enum>;`.
-  The debug formatter prints the binary flag value as well as the flag enums: `BitFlags(0b1111, [A, B, C, D])`.
-  Optional support for serialization with the `serde`

## Example

```
use ;
// Flags can be combined with |, this creates a BitFlags of your type:
let a_b:  = A | B;
let a_c = A | C;
let b_c_d = make_bitflags!;
// The debug output lets you inspect both the numeric value and
// the actual flags:
assert_eq!;
// But if you'd rather see only one of those, that's available too:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over the flags like a normal set
assert_eq!;
// Query the contents with contains and intersects
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
```
## Optional Feature Flags

- `serde`- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`for- `BitFlags<T>`.
- `std`implements- `std::error::Error`for- `FromBitsError`.

`const fn`-compatible APIs

**Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2632),
which makes it impossible to use any overloaded operators in a const
context.

**Naming convention:** If a separate, more limited function is provided
for usage in a `const fn`, the name is suffixed with `_c`.

Apart from functions whose name ends with `_c`, the [`make_bitflags!`] macro
is often useful for many `const` and `const fn` usecases.

**Blanket implementations:** If you attempt to write a `const fn` ranging
over `T: BitFlag`, you will be met with an error explaining that currently,
the only allowed trait bound for a `const fn` is `?Sized`. You will probably
want to write a separate implementation for `BitFlags<T, u8>`,
`BitFlags<T, u16>`, etc — best accomplished by a simple macro.

**Documentation considerations:** The strategy described above is often used
by `enumflags2` itself. To avoid clutter in the auto-generated documentation,
the implementations for widths other than `u8` are marked with `#[doc(hidden)]`.

## Customizing `Default`

By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result in an empty
set. If that's undesirable, you may customize this:

```
assert_eq!;
```

# Enumflags

`enumflags2` implements the classic bitflags datastructure. Annotate an enum

of your enum within the space of a single integer.

## Features

- Uses enums to represent individual flags—a set of flags is a separate type from a single flag.
- Automatically chooses a free bit when you don't specify.
- Detects incorrect BitFlags at compile time.
-  Has a similar API compared to the popular [bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags)crate.
-  Does not expose the generated types explicity. The user interacts exclusively with `struct BitFlags<Enum>;`.
-  The debug formatter prints the binary flag value as well as the flag enums: `BitFlags(0b1111, [A, B, C, D])`.

let a_b:  = A | B;
let a_c = A | C;
let b_c_d = make_bitflags!;
// The debug output lets you inspect both the numeric value and
// the actual flags:
assert_eq!;
// But if you'd rather see only one of those, that's available too:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over the flags like a normal set
assert_eq!;
// Query the contents with contains and intersects
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
```
## Optional Feature Flags

- `serde`- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`for- `BitFlags<T>`.
- `std`implements- `std::error::Error`for- `FromBitsError`.

`const fn`-compatible APIs

**Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2632),
which makes it impossible to use any overloaded operators in a const
context.

**Naming convention:** If a separate, more limited function is provided
for usage in a `const fn`, the name is suffixed with `_c`.

**Blanket implementations:** If you attempt to write a `const fn` ranging
over `T: BitFlag`, you will be met with an error explaining that currently,
the only allowed trait bound for a `const fn` is `?Sized`. You will probably
want to write a separate implementation for `BitFlags<T, u8>`,
`BitFlags<T, u16>`, etc — probably generated by a macro.
This strategy is often used by `enumflags2` itself; to avoid clutter, only
one of the copies is shown in the documentation.

## Customizing `Default`

By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result in an empty
set. If that's undesirable, you may customize this:

```
assert_eq!;
```

# enumflags2 0.7.7 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enumflags2/0.7.7

# Enumflags

`enumflags2` implements the classic bitflags datastructure. Annotate an enum
with `#[bitflags]`, and `BitFlags<YourEnum>` will be able to hold arbitrary combinations
of your enum within the space of a single integer.

## Features

- Uses enums to represent individual flags—a set of flags is a separate type from a single flag.
- Automatically chooses a free bit when you don't specify.
- Detects incorrect BitFlags at compile time.
-  Has a similar API compared to the popular [bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags)crate.
-  Does not expose the generated types explicity. The user interacts exclusively with `struct BitFlags<Enum>;`.
-  The debug formatter prints the binary flag value as well as the flag enums: `BitFlags(0b1111, [A, B, C, D])`.
-  Optional support for serialization with the `serde`

## Example

```
use ;
// Flags can be combined with |, this creates a BitFlags of your type:
let a_b:  = A | B;
let a_c = A | C;
let b_c_d = make_bitflags!;
// The debug output lets you inspect both the numeric value and
// the actual flags:
assert_eq!;
// But if you'd rather see only one of those, that's available too:
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// Iterate over the flags like a normal set
assert_eq!;
// Query the contents with contains and intersects
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
```
## Optional Feature Flags

- `serde`- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`for- `BitFlags<T>`.
- `std`implements- `std::error::Error`for- `FromBitsError`.

`const fn`-compatible APIs

**Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2632),

# enumflags2 0.7.0-preview1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enumflags2/0.7.0-preview1

# Enumflags

`enumflags2` defines a `BitFlags<T>` type, which is a `Set<T>`
for enums without associated data.

## Usage

In your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "^0.6"
```
## Features

- Uses enums to represent individual flags—a set of flags is a separate type from a single flag.
- Detects incorrect BitFlags at compile time.
-  Has a similar API compared to the popular [bitflags](https://crates.io/crates/bitflags)crate.
-  Does not expose the generated types explicity. The user interacts exclusively with `struct BitFlags<Enum>;`.
-  The debug formatter prints the binary flag value as well as the flag enums: `BitFlags(0b1111, [A, B, C, D])`.
-  Optional support for serialization with the `serde`

### Example

```
use BitFlags;
let a_b = A | B; // BitFlags<Test>
let a_c = A | C;
let b_c_d = C | B | D;
// BitFlags<Test>(0b11, [A, B])
println!;
// BitFlags<Test>(0b1, [A])
println!;
// Iterate over the flags like a normal set!
assert_eq!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
```
### Note

By default, the `BitFlags` are `usize`-sized. If you want them to be smaller,
specify a `repr` on your enum as in the example above.

### Migrating from 0.5

The minimum rustc version has been bumped to 1.34.0, because of `syn 1.0`. The
version policy from now on will be "what's available on Debian stable", [because
Debian is famously slow with new software versions](https://www.jwz.org/blog/2016/04/i-would-like-debian-to-stop-shipping-xscreensaver/).

You should no longer depend on `enumflags2_derive` directly.
Use the reexport from the `enumflags2` crate.
semver guarantees will be violated if you depend on the derive crate directly.

The derive macro has been renamed to `BitFlags`, to make it clearer what the
derive does.

The `nostd` feature flag has been removed. The crate now only depends on `libcore`
by default. Enable the `std` flag to get an implementation of `std::error::Error`
on error types.

Flags more than one bit set have been found to have inconsistent semantics.
They are now rejected at compile-time. The same applies to flags without any
bit set. If you were relying on this in your code, please [open an issue](https://github.com/NieDzejkob/enumflags2/issues/new)
and explain your usecase.

`BitFlags::from_bits` returns a `Result` instead of an `Option`. This might
necessitate some minor changes in your code.

`BitFlags::not` has been removed. Use the `!` operator instead.

---

// BitFlags<Test>(0b1, [A])
println!;
// Iterate over the flags like a normal set!
assert_eq!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
```
## Note

By default, the `BitFlags` are `usize`-sized. If you want them to be smaller,
specify a `repr` on your enum as in the example above.

## Optional Feature Flags

- `serde`- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`for- `BitFlags<T>`.
- `std`implements- `std::error::Error`for- `FromBitsError`.
- `not_literal`enables a workaround that allows using discriminant expressions that can't be evaluated at macro expansion time. Notably, this includes using pre-existing constants.

This is disabled by default because of the high potential for confusing error messages - if a flag doesn't have exactly one bit set, the error message will be "attempt to subtract with overflow", pointing at the relevant flag.

### Migrating from 0.5

The minimum rustc version has been bumped to 1.34.0, because of `syn 1.0`. The
version policy from now on will be "what's available on Debian stable", [because
Debian is famously slow with new software versions](https://www.jwz.org/blog/2016/04/i-would-like-debian-to-stop-shipping-xscreensaver/).

You should no longer depend on `enumflags2_derive` directly.
Use the reexport from the `enumflags2` crate.
semver guarantees will be violated if you depend on the derive crate directly.

The derive macro has been renamed to `BitFlags`, to make it clearer what the
derive does.

The `nostd` feature flag has been removed. The crate now only depends on `libcore`
by default. Enable the `std` flag to get an implementation of `std::error::Error`
on error types.

Flags more than one bit set have been found to have inconsistent semantics.
They are now rejected at compile-time. The same applies to flags without any
bit set. If you were relying on this in your code, please [open an issue](https://github.com/NieDzejkob/enumflags2/issues/new)
and explain your usecase.

`BitFlags::from_bits` returns a `Result` instead of an `Option`. This might
necessitate some minor changes in your code.

`BitFlags::not` has been removed. Use the `!` operator instead.

---

extern crate enumflags2;

use BitFlags;
```

# enumflags2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/enumflags2

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#enum-flags)Enum Flags

`enumflags2` implements the classic bitflags datastructure. Annotate an enum
with `#[bitflags]`, and `BitFlags<YourEnum>` will be able to hold arbitrary combinations
of your enum within the space of a single integer.

Unlike other crates, `enumflags2` makes the type-level distinction between
a single flag (`YourEnum`) and a set of flags (`BitFlags<YourEnum>`).
This allows idiomatic handling of bitflags, such as with `match` and `iter`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use enumflags2::{bitflags, make_bitflags, BitFlags};
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Test {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C, // unspecified variants pick unused bits automatically
    D = 0b1000,
}
// Flags can be combined with |, this creates a BitFlags of your type:
let a_b: BitFlags<Test> = Test::A | Test::B;
let a_c = Test::A | Test::C;
let b_c_d = make_bitflags!(Test::{B | C | D});
// The debug output lets you inspect both the numeric value and
// the actual flags:
assert_eq!(format!("{:?}", a_b), "BitFlags<Test>(0b11, A | B)");
// But if you'd rather see only one of those, that's available too:
assert_eq!(format!("{}", a_b), "A | B");
assert_eq!(format!("{:04b}", a_b), "0011");
// Iterate over the flags like a normal set
assert_eq!(a_b.iter().collect::<Vec<_>>(), &[Test::A, Test::B]);
// Query the contents with contains and intersects
assert!(a_b.contains(Test::A));
assert!(b_c_d.contains(Test::B | Test::C));
assert!(!(b_c_d.contains(a_b)));
assert!(a_b.intersects(a_c));
assert!(!(a_b.intersects(Test::C | Test::D)));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#optional-feature-flags)Optional Feature Flags

- `serde`- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`for- `BitFlags<T>`.
- `std`implements- `std::error::Error`for- `FromBitsError`.

[§](https://docs.rs#const-fn-compatible-apis)`const fn`-compatible APIs

**Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2632),
which makes it impossible to use any overloaded operators in a const
context.

**Naming convention:** If a separate, more limited function is provided
for usage in a `const fn`, the name is suffixed with `_c`.

Apart from functions whose name ends with `_c`, the [ make_bitflags!](https://docs.rs/macro.make_bitflags.html) macro
is often useful for many

`const` and `const fn` usecases.**Blanket implementations:** If you attempt to write a `const fn` ranging
over `T: BitFlag`, you will be met with an error explaining that currently,
the only allowed trait bound for a `const fn` is `?Sized`. You will probably
want to write a separate implementation for `BitFlags<T, u8>`,
`BitFlags<T, u16>`, etc — best accomplished by a simple macro.

**Documentation considerations:** The strategy described above is often used
by `enumflags2` itself. To avoid clutter in the auto-generated documentation,
the implementations for widths other than `u8` are marked with `#[doc(hidden)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#customizing-default)Customizing `Default`

By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result in an empty
set. If that’s undesirable, you may customize this:

```
#[bitflags(default = B | C)]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Test {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C = 0b0100,
    D = 0b1000,
}
assert_eq!(BitFlags::default(), Test::B | Test::C);
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [make_](https://docs.rs/macro.make_bitflags.html)- bitflags
- `make_bitflags!`provides a succint syntax for creating instances of- `BitFlags<T>`. Instead of repeating the name of your type for each flag you want to add, try- `make_bitflags!(Flags::{Foo | Bar})`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BitFlags](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html)
- Represents a set of flags of some type `T`.`T`must have the`#[bitflags]`attribute applied.
- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstToken.html)- Token
- Workaround for `const fn`limitations.
- [From](https://docs.rs/struct.FromBitsError.html)- Bits - Error
- The error struct used by `BitFlags::from_bits``TryFrom`
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- Iterator that yields each flag set in a `BitFlags`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [BitFlag](https://docs.rs/trait.BitFlag.html)
- A trait automatically implemented by `#[bitflags]`to make the enum a valid type parameter for`BitFlags<T>`.

# enumflags2 0.7.12 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enumflags2/latest/source/README.md

```
[![LICENSE](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE-MIT)
[![LICENSE](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-apache-blue.svg)](LICENSE-APACHE)
[![Documentation](https://docs.rs/enumflags2/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/enumflags2)
[![Crates.io Version](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/enumflags2.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/enumflags2)
`enumflags2` implements the classic bitflags datastructure. Annotate an enum
with `#[bitflags]`, and `BitFlags<YourEnum>` will be able to hold arbitrary combinations
of your enum within the space of a single integer.
Unlike other crates, `enumflags2` makes the type-level distinction between
a single flag (`YourEnum`) and a set of flags (`BitFlags<YourEnum>`).
This allows idiomatic handling of bitflags, such as with `match` and `iter`.
- ------
```rust
use enumflags2::{bitflags, make_bitflags, BitFlags};
enum Test {
}
// The debug output lets you inspect both the numeric value and
// the actual flags:
// Iterate over the flags like a normal set
assert_eq!(a_b.iter().collect::<Vec<_>>(), &[Test::A, Test::B]);
// Query the contents with contains and intersects
assert!(a_b.contains(Test::A));
assert!(a_b.intersects(a_c));
assert!(!(a_b.intersects(Test::C | Test::D)));
```
- -
**Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage][const-trait-rfc],
which makes it impossible to use any overloaded operators in a const
context.
**Naming convention:** If a separate, more limited function is provided
for usage in a `const fn`, the name is suffixed with `_c`.
Apart from functions whose name ends with `_c`, the [`make_bitflags!`] macro
is often useful for many `const` and `const fn` usecases.
**Blanket implementations:** If you attempt to write a `const fn` ranging
over `T: BitFlag`, you will be met with an error explaining that currently,
the only allowed trait bound for a `const fn` is `?Sized`. You will probably
want to write a separate implementation for `BitFlags<T, u8>`,
`BitFlags<T, u16>`, etc — best accomplished by a simple macro.
**Documentation considerations:** The strategy described above is often used
by `enumflags2` itself. To avoid clutter in the auto-generated documentation,
the implementations for widths other than `u8` are marked with `#[doc(hidden)]`.
By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result in an empty
set. If that's undesirable, you may customize this:
```rust
enum Test {
}
assert_eq!(BitFlags::default(), Test::B | Test::C);
```
```

# proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1.0/

## Expand description

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler’s [ proc_macro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/index.html)
crate. This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
#[proc_macro_derive(MyDerive)]
pub fn my_derive(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    let input = proc_macro2::TokenStream::from(input);
    let output: proc_macro2::TokenStream = {
        /* transform input */
    };
    proc_macro::TokenStream::from(output)
}
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you’ll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to
propagate parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable
compiler API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not
exposed by proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly
compiler, the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to
rustc. We will polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As
these are unstable APIs that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of
proc-macro2 may make breaking changes to them at any time.

`RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build`Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-safety)Thread-Safety

Most types in this crate are `!Sync` because the underlying compiler
types make use of thread-local memory, meaning they cannot be accessed from
a different thread.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/^1.0/

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.

---

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2.0/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

# serde_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/=1.0.228/

## Expand description

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The `serde_core` crate contains Serde’s trait definitions with **no support
for #[derive()]**.

In crates that derive an implementation of `Serialize` or `Deserialize`, you
must depend on the [ serde](https://crates.io/crates/serde) crate, not

`serde_core`.In crates that handwrite implementations of Serde traits, or only use them
as trait bounds, depending on `serde_core` is permitted. But `serde`
re-exports all of these traits and can be used for this use case too. If in
doubt, disregard `serde_core` and always use `serde`.

Crates that depend on `serde_core` instead of `serde` are able to compile in
parallel with `serde_derive` even when `serde`’s “derive” feature is turned on,
as shown in the following build timings.

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde` |

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde_core` |

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/serde/1.0.228/target-redirect/serde/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)
