}## Expand description

A **data format** that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

The role of this trait is to define the serialization half of the [Serde
data model](https://serde.rs/data-model.html), which is a way to categorize every Rust data structure into one
of 29 possible types. Each method of the `Serializer` trait corresponds to
one of the types of the data model.

Implementations of `Serialize` map themselves into this data model by
invoking exactly one of the `Serializer` methods.

The types that make up the Serde data model are:

- **14 primitive types**- bool
- i8, i16, i32, i64, i128
- u8, u16, u32, u64, u128
- f32, f64
- char

- **string**- UTF-8 bytes with a length and no null terminator.
- When serializing, all strings are handled equally. When deserializing, there are three flavors of strings: transient, owned, and borrowed.

- **byte array**- [u8]- Similar to strings, during deserialization byte arrays can be transient, owned, or borrowed.

- **option**- Either none or some value.

- **unit**- The type of `()`in Rust. It represents an anonymous value containing no data.

- The type of
- **unit_struct**- For example `struct Unit`or`PhantomData<T>`. It represents a named value containing no data.

- For example
- **unit_variant**- For example the `E::A`and`E::B`in`enum E { A, B }`.

- For example the
- **newtype_struct**- For example `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

- For example
- **newtype_variant**- For example the `E::N`in`enum E { N(u8) }`.

- For example the
- **seq**- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
`Vec<T>`or`HashSet<T>`. When serializing, the length may or may not be known before iterating through all the data. When deserializing, the length is determined by looking at the serialized data.

- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
- **tuple**- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `(u8,)`or`(String, u64, Vec<T>)`or`[u64; 10]`.

- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **tuple_struct**- A named tuple, for example `struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8)`.

- A named tuple, for example
- **tuple_variant**- For example the `E::T`in`enum E { T(u8, u8) }`.

- For example the
- **map**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example `BTreeMap<K, V>`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example
- **struct**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `struct S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **struct_variant**- For example the `E::S`in`enum E { S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 } }`.

- For example the

Many Serde serializers produce text or binary data as output, for example
JSON or Postcard. This is not a requirement of the `Serializer` trait, and
there are serializers that do not produce text or binary output. One example
is the `serde_json::value::Serializer` (distinct from the main `serde_json`
serializer) that produces a `serde_json::Value` data structure in memory as
output.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-implementation)Example implementation

The [example data format](https://serde.rs/data-format.html) presented on the website contains example code for
a basic JSON `Serializer`.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

The output type produced by this `Serializer` during successful
serialization. Most serializers that produce text or binary output
should set `Ok = ()` and serialize into an [ io::Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html) or buffer
contained within the

`Serializer` instance. Serializers that build
in-memory data structures may be simplified by using `Ok` to propagate
the data structure around.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize an `i8` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i8` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize an `i16` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i16` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize an `i32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i32` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize a `u8` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u8` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize a `u16` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u16` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize a `u32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u32` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize an `f32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `f32` and `f64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `f64` and
forward to `serialize_f64`.

Serialize a character.

If the format does not support characters, it is reasonable to serialize
it as a single element `str` or a `u32`.

Serialize a chunk of raw byte data.

Enables serializers to serialize byte slices more compactly or more
efficiently than other types of slices. If no efficient implementation
is available, a reasonable implementation would be to forward to
`serialize_seq`. If forwarded, the implementation looks usually just
like this:

Serialize a unit struct like `struct Unit` or `PhantomData<T>`.

A reasonable implementation would be to forward to `serialize_unit`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct Nothing;
impl Serialize for Nothing {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.serialize_unit_struct("Nothing")
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#889-894)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#889-894)

Serialize a unit variant like `E::A` in `enum E { A, B }`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, and the `variant` is the name of the
variant.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
enum E {
    A,
    B,
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::A => serializer.serialize_unit_variant("E", 0, "A"),
            E::B => serializer.serialize_unit_variant("E", 1, "B"),
        }
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#916-922)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#916-922)

Serialize a newtype struct like `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

Serializers are encouraged to treat newtype structs as insignificant
wrappers around the data they contain. A reasonable implementation would
be to forward to `value.serialize(self)`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct Millimeters(u8);
impl Serialize for Millimeters {

        S: Serializer,

Begin to serialize a variably sized sequence. This call must be
followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_element`, then a call to
`end`.

The argument is the number of elements in the sequence, which may or may not be computable before the sequence is iterated. Some serializers only support sequences whose length is known up front.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeSeq, Serializer};
impl<T> Serialize for Vec<T>
where
    T: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut seq = serializer.serialize_seq(Some(self.len()))?;
        for element in self {
            seq.serialize_element(element)?;
        }
        seq.end()
    }
}
```

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```

impl<A, B, C> Serialize for (A, B, C)
where
    A: Serialize,
    B: Serialize,
    C: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut tup = serializer.serialize_tuple(3)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.0)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.1)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.2)?;
        tup.end()
    }
}

    K: Serialize,
    V: Serialize,

    where
        S: Serializer,

        for (k, v) in self {
            map.serialize_entry(k, v)?;

        map.end()

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1459-1461)#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde/core/ser/mod.rs.html#1459-1461)

#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

Determine whether `Serialize` implementations should serialize in
human-readable form.

Some types have a human-readable form that may be somewhat expensive to construct, as well as a binary form that is compact and efficient. Generally text-based formats like JSON and YAML will prefer to use the human-readable one and binary formats like Postcard will prefer the compact one.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
impl Serialize for Timestamp {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        if serializer.is_human_readable() {
            // Serialize to a human-readable string "2015-05-15T17:01:00Z".
            self.to_string().serialize(serializer)
        } else {
            // Serialize to a compact binary representation.
            self.seconds_since_epoch().serialize(serializer)
        }
    }
}
```
The default implementation of this method returns `true`. Data formats
may override this to `false` to request a compact form for types that
support one. Note that modifying this method to change a format from
human-readable to compact or vice versa should be regarded as a breaking
change, as a value serialized in human-readable mode is not required to
deserialize from the same data in compact mode.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# enumflags2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enumflags2/latest/target-redirect/enumflags2/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#enum-flags)Enum Flags

`enumflags2` implements the classic bitflags datastructure. Annotate an enum
with `#[bitflags]`, and `BitFlags<YourEnum>` will be able to hold arbitrary combinations
of your enum within the space of a single integer.

Unlike other crates, `enumflags2` makes the type-level distinction between
a single flag (`YourEnum`) and a set of flags (`BitFlags<YourEnum>`).
This allows idiomatic handling of bitflags, such as with `match` and `iter`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use enumflags2::{bitflags, make_bitflags, BitFlags};
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Test {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C, // unspecified variants pick unused bits automatically
    D = 0b1000,
}
// Flags can be combined with |, this creates a BitFlags of your type:
let a_b: BitFlags<Test> = Test::A | Test::B;
let a_c = Test::A | Test::C;
let b_c_d = make_bitflags!(Test::{B | C | D});
// The debug output lets you inspect both the numeric value and
// the actual flags:
assert_eq!(format!("{:?}", a_b), "BitFlags<Test>(0b11, A | B)");
// But if you'd rather see only one of those, that's available too:
assert_eq!(format!("{}", a_b), "A | B");
assert_eq!(format!("{:04b}", a_b), "0011");
// Iterate over the flags like a normal set
assert_eq!(a_b.iter().collect::<Vec<_>>(), &[Test::A, Test::B]);
// Query the contents with contains and intersects
assert!(a_b.contains(Test::A));
assert!(b_c_d.contains(Test::B | Test::C));
assert!(!(b_c_d.contains(a_b)));
assert!(a_b.intersects(a_c));
assert!(!(a_b.intersects(Test::C | Test::D)));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#optional-feature-flags)Optional Feature Flags

- `serde`- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`for- `BitFlags<T>`.
- `std`implements- `std::error::Error`for- `FromBitsError`.

[§](https://docs.rs#const-fn-compatible-apis)`const fn`-compatible APIs

**Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2632),
which makes it impossible to use any overloaded operators in a const
context.

**Naming convention:** If a separate, more limited function is provided
for usage in a `const fn`, the name is suffixed with `_c`.

Apart from functions whose name ends with `_c`, the [ make_bitflags!](https://docs.rs/macro.make_bitflags.html) macro
is often useful for many

`const` and `const fn` usecases.**Blanket implementations:** If you attempt to write a `const fn` ranging
over `T: BitFlag`, you will be met with an error explaining that currently,
the only allowed trait bound for a `const fn` is `?Sized`. You will probably
want to write a separate implementation for `BitFlags<T, u8>`,
`BitFlags<T, u16>`, etc — best accomplished by a simple macro.

**Documentation considerations:** The strategy described above is often used
by `enumflags2` itself. To avoid clutter in the auto-generated documentation,
the implementations for widths other than `u8` are marked with `#[doc(hidden)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#customizing-default)Customizing `Default`

By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result in an empty
set. If that’s undesirable, you may customize this:

```
#[bitflags(default = B | C)]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Test {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C = 0b0100,
    D = 0b1000,
}
assert_eq!(BitFlags::default(), Test::B | Test::C);
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [make_](https://docs.rs/macro.make_bitflags.html)- bitflags
- `make_bitflags!`provides a succint syntax for creating instances of- `BitFlags<T>`. Instead of repeating the name of your type for each flag you want to add, try- `make_bitflags!(Flags::{Foo | Bar})`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BitFlags](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html)
- Represents a set of flags of some type `T`.`T`must have the`#[bitflags]`attribute applied.
- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstToken.html)- Token
- Workaround for `const fn`limitations.
- [From](https://docs.rs/struct.FromBitsError.html)- Bits - Error
- The error struct used by `BitFlags::from_bits``TryFrom`
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- Iterator that yields each flag set in a `BitFlags`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [BitFlag](https://docs.rs/trait.BitFlag.html)
- A trait automatically implemented by `#[bitflags]`to make the enum a valid type parameter for`BitFlags<T>`.

# enumflags2/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # Enum Flags
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! `enumflags2` implements the classic bitflags datastructure. Annotate an enum
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! with `#[bitflags]`, and `BitFlags<YourEnum>` will be able to hold arbitrary combinations
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! of your enum within the space of a single integer.
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! Unlike other crates, `enumflags2` makes the type-level distinction between
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! a single flag (`YourEnum`) and a set of flags (`BitFlags<YourEnum>`).
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! This allows idiomatic handling of bitflags, such as with `match` and `iter`.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! ## Example
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! ```
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! use enumflags2::{bitflags, make_bitflags, BitFlags};
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! #[bitflags]
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! #[repr(u8)]
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! enum Test {
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!     A = 0b0001,
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!     B = 0b0010,
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!     C, // unspecified variants pick unused bits automatically
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!     D = 0b1000,
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! }
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! // Flags can be combined with |, this creates a BitFlags of your type:
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! let a_b: BitFlags<Test> = Test::A | Test::B;
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! let a_c = Test::A | Test::C;
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! let b_c_d = make_bitflags!(Test::{B | C | D});
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! // The debug output lets you inspect both the numeric value and
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! // the actual flags:
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! assert_eq!(format!("{:?}", a_b), "BitFlags<Test>(0b11, A | B)");
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! // But if you'd rather see only one of those, that's available too:
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! assert_eq!(format!("{}", a_b), "A | B");
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! assert_eq!(format!("{:04b}", a_b), "0011");
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! // Iterate over the flags like a normal set
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! assert_eq!(a_b.iter().collect::<Vec<_>>(), &[Test::A, Test::B]);
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! // Query the contents with contains and intersects
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! assert!(a_b.contains(Test::A));
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! assert!(b_c_d.contains(Test::B | Test::C));
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! assert!(!(b_c_d.contains(a_b)));
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! assert!(a_b.intersects(a_c));
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! assert!(!(a_b.intersects(Test::C | Test::D)));
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! ```
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! ## Optional Feature Flags
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! - [`serde`](https://serde.rs/) implements `Serialize` and `Deserialize`
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!   for `BitFlags<T>`.
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! - `std` implements `std::error::Error` for `FromBitsError`.
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! ## `const fn`-compatible APIs
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! **Background:** The subset of `const fn` features currently stabilized is pretty limited.
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! Most notably, [const traits are still at the RFC stage][const-trait-rfc],
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! which makes it impossible to use any overloaded operators in a const
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! context.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! **Naming convention:** If a separate, more limited function is provided
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! for usage in a `const fn`, the name is suffixed with `_c`.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! Apart from functions whose name ends with `_c`, the [`make_bitflags!`] macro
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! is often useful for many `const` and `const fn` usecases.
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! **Blanket implementations:** If you attempt to write a `const fn` ranging
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! over `T: BitFlag`, you will be met with an error explaining that currently,
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! the only allowed trait bound for a `const fn` is `?Sized`. You will probably
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! want to write a separate implementation for `BitFlags<T, u8>`,
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! `BitFlags<T, u16>`, etc — best accomplished by a simple macro.
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! **Documentation considerations:** The strategy described above is often used
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! by `enumflags2` itself. To avoid clutter in the auto-generated documentation,
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! the implementations for widths other than `u8` are marked with `#[doc(hidden)]`.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! ## Customizing `Default`
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result in an empty
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! set. If that's undesirable, you may customize this:
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! ```
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! # use enumflags2::{BitFlags, bitflags};
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! #[bitflags(default = B | C)]
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! #[repr(u8)]
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! enum Test {
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!     A = 0b0001,
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!     B = 0b0010,
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!     C = 0b0100,
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!     D = 0b1000,
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! }
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! assert_eq!(BitFlags::default(), Test::B | Test::C);
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! ```
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//!
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! [const-trait-rfc]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2632
[99](https://docs.rs#99)#![warn(missing_docs)]
[100](https://docs.rs#100)#![cfg_attr(all(not(test), not(feature = "std")), no_std)]

[113](https://docs.rs#113)// Internal macro: expand into a separate copy for each supported numeric type.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)macro_rules! for_each_uint {
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    ( $d:tt $tyvar:ident $dd:tt $docattr:ident => $($input:tt)* ) => {
[116](https://docs.rs#116)        macro_rules! implement {
[117](https://docs.rs#117)            ( $d $tyvar:ty => $d($d $docattr:meta)? ) => {
[118](https://docs.rs#118)                $($input)*
[119](https://docs.rs#119)            }
[120](https://docs.rs#120)        }
[121](https://docs.rs#121)
[122](https://docs.rs#122)        implement! { u8 => }
[123](https://docs.rs#123)        implement! { u16 => doc(hidden) }
[124](https://docs.rs#124)        implement! { u32 => doc(hidden) }
[125](https://docs.rs#125)        implement! { u64 => doc(hidden) }
[126](https://docs.rs#126)        implement! { u128 => doc(hidden) }
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    }

[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// A trait automatically implemented by `#[bitflags]` to make the enum
[131](https://docs.rs#131)/// a valid type parameter for `BitFlags<T>`.
[132](https://docs.rs#132)pub trait BitFlag: Copy + Clone + 'static + _internal::RawBitFlags {
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    /// Create a `BitFlags` with no flags set (in other words, with a value of 0).
[134](https://docs.rs#134)    ///
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    /// This is a convenience reexport of [`BitFlags::empty`]. It can be called with
[136](https://docs.rs#136)    /// `MyFlag::empty()`, thus bypassing the need for type hints in some situations.
[137](https://docs.rs#137)    ///
[138](https://docs.rs#138)    /// ```
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    /// #[bitflags]
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[142](https://docs.rs#142)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    /// enum MyFlag {
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[145](https://docs.rs#145)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    /// }
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    ///
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    /// use enumflags2::BitFlag;
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    ///
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    /// let empty = MyFlag::empty();
[152](https://docs.rs#152)    /// assert!(empty.is_empty());
[153](https://docs.rs#153)    /// assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::One), false);
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    /// assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::Two), false);
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    /// assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    /// ```
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    #[inline]
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    fn empty() -> BitFlags<Self> {
[159](https://docs.rs#159)        BitFlags::empty()
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    }
[161](https://docs.rs#161)
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    /// Create a `BitFlags` with all flags set.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    ///
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    /// This is a convenience reexport of [`BitFlags::all`]. It can be called with
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    /// `MyFlag::all()`, thus bypassing the need for type hints in some situations.
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    ///
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    /// ```
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    /// #[bitflags]
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// enum MyFlag {
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// }
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    ///
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    /// use enumflags2::BitFlag;
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    ///
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// let all = MyFlag::all();
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    /// assert!(all.is_all());
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    /// assert_eq!(all.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    /// assert_eq!(all.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    /// assert_eq!(all.contains(MyFlag::Three), true);
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    /// ```
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    #[inline]
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    fn all() -> BitFlags<Self> {
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        BitFlags::all()
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    }
[190](https://docs.rs#190)
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    /// Create a `BitFlags` if the raw value provided does not contain
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    /// any illegal flags.
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    ///
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    /// This is a convenience reexport of [`BitFlags::from_bits`]. It can be called
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    /// with `MyFlag::from_bits(bits)`, thus bypassing the need for type hints in
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    /// some situations.
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    ///
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    /// ```
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    /// #[bitflags]
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    /// enum MyFlag {
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    /// }
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    ///
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    /// use enumflags2::BitFlag;
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    ///
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    /// let flags = MyFlag::from_bits(0b11).unwrap();
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    /// let invalid = MyFlag::from_bits(1 << 3);
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    /// assert!(invalid.is_err());
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    /// ```
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    #[inline]
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    fn from_bits(bits: Self::Numeric) -> Result<BitFlags<Self>, FromBitsError<Self>> {
[220](https://docs.rs#220)        BitFlags::from_bits(bits)
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    }
[222](https://docs.rs#222)
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    /// Create a `BitFlags` from an underlying bitwise value. If any
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// invalid bits are set, ignore them.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    ///
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    /// This is a convenience reexport of [`BitFlags::from_bits_truncate`]. It can be
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    /// called with `MyFlag::from_bits_truncate(bits)`, thus bypassing the need for
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// type hints in some situations.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    ///
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    /// ```
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// #[bitflags]
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    /// enum MyFlag {
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    /// }
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    ///
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// use enumflags2::BitFlag;
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    ///
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    /// let flags = MyFlag::from_bits_truncate(0b1_1011);
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    /// ```
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    #[inline]
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    fn from_bits_truncate(bits: Self::Numeric) -> BitFlags<Self> {
[250](https://docs.rs#250)        BitFlags::from_bits_truncate(bits)
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    }
[252](https://docs.rs#252)
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    /// Create a `BitFlags` unsafely, without checking if the bits form
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    /// a valid bit pattern for the type.
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    ///
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    /// Consider using [`from_bits`][BitFlag::from_bits]
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// or [`from_bits_truncate`][BitFlag::from_bits_truncate] instead.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    /// # Safety
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    ///
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// All bits set in `val` must correspond to a value of the enum.
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    ///
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    /// # Example
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    ///
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    /// This is a convenience reexport of [`BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked`]. It can be
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    /// called with `MyFlag::from_bits_unchecked(bits)`, thus bypassing the need for
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// type hints in some situations.
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    ///
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// ```
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    /// #[bitflags]
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// enum MyFlag {
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    /// }
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    ///
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    /// use enumflags2::BitFlag;
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    ///
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    /// let flags = unsafe {
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    ///     MyFlag::from_bits_unchecked(0b011)
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    /// };
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    ///
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    /// ```
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    #[inline]
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    unsafe fn from_bits_unchecked(bits: Self::Numeric) -> BitFlags<Self> {
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked(bits)
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    }

[296](https://docs.rs#296)/// While the module is public, this is only the case because it needs to be
[297](https://docs.rs#297)/// accessed by the macro. Do not use this directly. Stability guarantees
[298](https://docs.rs#298)/// don't apply.
[299](https://docs.rs#299)#[doc(hidden)]
[300](https://docs.rs#300)pub mod _internal {
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    /// A trait automatically implemented by `#[bitflags]` to make the enum
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    /// a valid type parameter for `BitFlags<T>`.
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    ///
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    /// # Safety
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    ///
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    /// The values should reflect reality, like they do if the implementation
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    /// is generated by the procmacro.
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    ///
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    /// `bits` must return the same value as
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    /// [`transmute_copy`][std::mem::transmute_copy].
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    ///
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    /// Representations for all values of `T` must have exactly one bit set.
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    pub unsafe trait RawBitFlags: Copy + Clone + 'static {
[314](https://docs.rs#314)        /// The underlying integer type.
[315](https://docs.rs#315)        type Numeric: BitFlagNum;
[316](https://docs.rs#316)
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        /// A value with no bits set.
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        const EMPTY: Self::Numeric;
[319](https://docs.rs#319)
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        /// The value used by the Default implementation. Equivalent to EMPTY, unless
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        /// customized.
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        const DEFAULT: Self::Numeric;
[323](https://docs.rs#323)
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        /// A value with all flag bits set.
[325](https://docs.rs#325)        const ALL_BITS: Self::Numeric;
[326](https://docs.rs#326)
[327](https://docs.rs#327)        /// The name of the type for debug formatting purposes.
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        ///
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        /// This is typically `BitFlags<EnumName>`
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        const BITFLAGS_TYPE_NAME: &'static str;
[331](https://docs.rs#331)
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        /// Return the bits as a number type.
[333](https://docs.rs#333)        fn bits(self) -> Self::Numeric;
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    }
[335](https://docs.rs#335)
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    use ::core::fmt;
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    use ::core::ops::{BitAnd, BitOr, BitXor, Not, Sub};
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    use ::core::hash::Hash;
[339](https://docs.rs#339)
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    pub trait BitFlagNum:
[341](https://docs.rs#341)        Default
[342](https://docs.rs#342)        + BitOr<Self, Output = Self>
[343](https://docs.rs#343)        + BitAnd<Self, Output = Self>
[344](https://docs.rs#344)        + BitXor<Self, Output = Self>
[345](https://docs.rs#345)        + Sub<Self, Output = Self>
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        + Not<Output = Self>
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        + PartialOrd<Self>
[348](https://docs.rs#348)        + Ord
[349](https://docs.rs#349)        + Hash
[350](https://docs.rs#350)        + fmt::Debug
[351](https://docs.rs#351)        + fmt::Binary
[352](https://docs.rs#352)        + Copy
[353](https://docs.rs#353)        + Clone
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    {
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        const ONE: Self;
[356](https://docs.rs#356)
[357](https://docs.rs#357)        fn is_power_of_two(self) -> bool;
[358](https://docs.rs#358)        fn count_ones(self) -> u32;
[359](https://docs.rs#359)        fn wrapping_neg(self) -> Self;
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    }

[425](https://docs.rs#425)
[426](https://docs.rs#426)/// Represents a set of flags of some type `T`.
[427](https://docs.rs#427)/// `T` must have the `#[bitflags]` attribute applied.
[428](https://docs.rs#428)///
[429](https://docs.rs#429)/// A `BitFlags<T>` is as large as the `T` itself,
[430](https://docs.rs#430)/// and stores one flag per bit.
[431](https://docs.rs#431)///
[432](https://docs.rs#432)/// ## Comparison operators, [`PartialOrd`] and [`Ord`]
[433](https://docs.rs#433)///
[434](https://docs.rs#434)/// To make it possible to use `BitFlags` as the key of a
[435](https://docs.rs#435)/// [`BTreeMap`][std::collections::BTreeMap], `BitFlags` implements
[436](https://docs.rs#436)/// [`Ord`]. There is no meaningful total order for bitflags,
[437](https://docs.rs#437)/// so the implementation simply compares the integer values of the bits.
[438](https://docs.rs#438)///
[439](https://docs.rs#439)/// Unfortunately, this means that comparing `BitFlags` with an operator
[440](https://docs.rs#440)/// like `<=` will compile, and return values that are probably useless
[441](https://docs.rs#441)/// and not what you expect. In particular, `<=` does *not* check whether
[442](https://docs.rs#442)/// one value is a subset of the other. Use [`BitFlags::contains`] for that.
[443](https://docs.rs#443)///
[444](https://docs.rs#444)/// ## Customizing `Default`
[445](https://docs.rs#445)///
[446](https://docs.rs#446)/// By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result
[447](https://docs.rs#447)/// in an empty set. If that's undesirable, you may customize this:
[448](https://docs.rs#448)///
[449](https://docs.rs#449)/// ```
[450](https://docs.rs#450)/// # use enumflags2::{BitFlags, bitflags};
[451](https://docs.rs#451)/// #[bitflags(default = B | C)]
[452](https://docs.rs#452)/// #[repr(u8)]
[453](https://docs.rs#453)/// #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
[454](https://docs.rs#454)/// enum MyFlag {
[455](https://docs.rs#455)///     A = 0b0001,
[456](https://docs.rs#456)///     B = 0b0010,
[457](https://docs.rs#457)///     C = 0b0100,
[458](https://docs.rs#458)///     D = 0b1000,
[459](https://docs.rs#459)/// }
[460](https://docs.rs#460)///
[461](https://docs.rs#461)/// assert_eq!(BitFlags::default(), MyFlag::B | MyFlag::C);
[462](https://docs.rs#462)/// ```
[463](https://docs.rs#463)///
[464](https://docs.rs#464)/// ## Memory layout
[465](https://docs.rs#465)///
[466](https://docs.rs#466)/// `BitFlags<T>` is marked with the `#[repr(transparent)]` trait, meaning
[467](https://docs.rs#467)/// it can be safely transmuted into the corresponding numeric type.
[468](https://docs.rs#468)///
[469](https://docs.rs#469)/// Usually, the same can be achieved by using [`BitFlags::bits`] in one
[470](https://docs.rs#470)/// direction, and [`BitFlags::from_bits`], [`BitFlags::from_bits_truncate`],
[471](https://docs.rs#471)/// or [`BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked`] in the other direction. However,
[472](https://docs.rs#472)/// transmuting might still be useful if, for example, you're dealing with
[473](https://docs.rs#473)/// an entire array of `BitFlags`.
[474](https://docs.rs#474)///
[475](https://docs.rs#475)/// When transmuting *into* a `BitFlags`, make sure that each set bit
[476](https://docs.rs#476)/// corresponds to an existing flag
[477](https://docs.rs#477)/// (cf. [`from_bits_unchecked`][BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked]).
[478](https://docs.rs#478)///
[479](https://docs.rs#479)/// For example:
[480](https://docs.rs#480)///
[481](https://docs.rs#481)/// ```
[482](https://docs.rs#482)/// # use enumflags2::{BitFlags, bitflags};
[483](https://docs.rs#483)/// #[bitflags]
[484](https://docs.rs#484)/// #[repr(u8)] // <-- the repr determines the numeric type
[485](https://docs.rs#485)/// #[derive(Copy, Clone)]
[486](https://docs.rs#486)/// enum TransmuteMe {
[487](https://docs.rs#487)///     One = 1 << 0,
[488](https://docs.rs#488)///     Two = 1 << 1,
[489](https://docs.rs#489)/// }
[490](https://docs.rs#490)///
[491](https://docs.rs#491)/// # use std::slice;
[492](https://docs.rs#492)/// // NOTE: we use a small, self-contained function to handle the slice
[493](https://docs.rs#493)/// // conversion to make sure the lifetimes are right.
[494](https://docs.rs#494)/// fn transmute_slice<'a>(input: &'a [BitFlags<TransmuteMe>]) -> &'a [u8] {
[495](https://docs.rs#495)///     unsafe {
[496](https://docs.rs#496)///         slice::from_raw_parts(input.as_ptr() as *const u8, input.len())
[497](https://docs.rs#497)///     }
[498](https://docs.rs#498)/// }
[499](https://docs.rs#499)///
[500](https://docs.rs#500)/// let many_flags = &[
[501](https://docs.rs#501)///     TransmuteMe::One.into(),
[502](https://docs.rs#502)///     TransmuteMe::One | TransmuteMe::Two,
[503](https://docs.rs#503)/// ];
[504](https://docs.rs#504)///
[505](https://docs.rs#505)/// let as_nums = transmute_slice(many_flags);
[506](https://docs.rs#506)/// assert_eq!(as_nums, &[0b01, 0b11]);
[507](https://docs.rs#507)/// ```
[508](https://docs.rs#508)///
[509](https://docs.rs#509)/// ## Implementation notes
[510](https://docs.rs#510)///
[511](https://docs.rs#511)/// You might expect this struct to be defined as
[512](https://docs.rs#512)///
[513](https://docs.rs#513)/// ```ignore
[514](https://docs.rs#514)/// struct BitFlags<T: BitFlag> {
[515](https://docs.rs#515)///     value: T::Numeric
[516](https://docs.rs#516)/// }
[517](https://docs.rs#517)/// ```
[518](https://docs.rs#518)///
[519](https://docs.rs#519)/// Ideally, that would be the case. However, because `const fn`s cannot
[520](https://docs.rs#520)/// have trait bounds in current Rust, this would prevent us from providing
[521](https://docs.rs#521)/// most `const fn` APIs. As a workaround, we define `BitFlags` with two
[522](https://docs.rs#522)/// type parameters, with a default for the second one:
[523](https://docs.rs#523)///
[524](https://docs.rs#524)/// ```ignore
[525](https://docs.rs#525)/// struct BitFlags<T, N = <T as BitFlag>::Numeric> {
[526](https://docs.rs#526)///     value: N,
[527](https://docs.rs#527)///     marker: PhantomData<T>,
[528](https://docs.rs#528)/// }
[529](https://docs.rs#529)/// ```
[530](https://docs.rs#530)///
[531](https://docs.rs#531)/// Manually providing a type for the `N` type parameter shouldn't ever
[532](https://docs.rs#532)/// be necessary.
[533](https://docs.rs#533)///
[534](https://docs.rs#534)/// The types substituted for `T` and `N` must always match, creating a
[535](https://docs.rs#535)/// `BitFlags` value where that isn't the case is only possible with
[536](https://docs.rs#536)/// incorrect unsafe code.
[537](https://docs.rs#537)#[derive(Copy, Clone)]
[538](https://docs.rs#538)#[repr(transparent)]
[539](https://docs.rs#539)pub struct BitFlags<T, N = <T as _internal::RawBitFlags>::Numeric> {
[540](https://docs.rs#540)    val: N,
[541](https://docs.rs#541)    marker: PhantomData<T>,
[542](https://docs.rs#542)}
[543](https://docs.rs#543)
[544](https://docs.rs#544)/// `make_bitflags!` provides a succint syntax for creating instances of
[545](https://docs.rs#545)/// `BitFlags<T>`. Instead of repeating the name of your type for each flag
[546](https://docs.rs#546)/// you want to add, try `make_bitflags!(Flags::{Foo | Bar})`.
[547](https://docs.rs#547)/// ```
[548](https://docs.rs#548)/// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags, make_bitflags};
[549](https://docs.rs#549)/// # #[bitflags]
[550](https://docs.rs#550)/// # #[repr(u8)]
[551](https://docs.rs#551)/// # #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
[552](https://docs.rs#552)/// # enum Test {
[553](https://docs.rs#553)/// #     A = 1 << 0,
[554](https://docs.rs#554)/// #     B = 1 << 1,
[555](https://docs.rs#555)/// #     C = 1 << 2,
[556](https://docs.rs#556)/// # }
[557](https://docs.rs#557)/// let x = make_bitflags!(Test::{A | C});
[558](https://docs.rs#558)/// assert_eq!(x, Test::A | Test::C);
[559](https://docs.rs#559)///
[560](https://docs.rs#560)/// // Also works in const contexts:
[561](https://docs.rs#561)/// const X: BitFlags<Test> = make_bitflags!(Test::A);
[562](https://docs.rs#562)/// ```
[563](https://docs.rs#563)#[macro_export]
[564](https://docs.rs#564)macro_rules! make_bitflags {
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    ( $enum:ident ::{ $($variant:ident)|* } ) => {
[566](https://docs.rs#566)        {
[567](https://docs.rs#567)            let mut n = 0;
[568](https://docs.rs#568)            $(
[569](https://docs.rs#569)                {
[570](https://docs.rs#570)                    let flag: $enum = $enum::$variant;
[571](https://docs.rs#571)                    n |= flag as <$enum as $crate::_internal::RawBitFlags>::Numeric;
[572](https://docs.rs#572)                }
[573](https://docs.rs#573)            )*
[574](https://docs.rs#574)            // SAFETY: The value has been created from numeric values of the underlying
[575](https://docs.rs#575)            // enum, so only valid bits are set.
[576](https://docs.rs#576)            unsafe { $crate::BitFlags::<$enum>::from_bits_unchecked_c(
[577](https://docs.rs#577)                    n, $crate::BitFlags::CONST_TOKEN) }
[578](https://docs.rs#578)        }
[579](https://docs.rs#579)    };
[580](https://docs.rs#580)    ( $enum:ident :: $variant:ident ) => {
[581](https://docs.rs#581)        {
[582](https://docs.rs#582)            let flag: $enum = $enum::$variant;
[583](https://docs.rs#583)            let n = flag as <$enum as $crate::_internal::RawBitFlags>::Numeric;
[584](https://docs.rs#584)            // SAFETY: The value has been created from the numeric value of
[585](https://docs.rs#585)            // the underlying enum, so only valid bits are set.
[586](https://docs.rs#586)            unsafe { $crate::BitFlags::<$enum>::from_bits_unchecked_c(
[587](https://docs.rs#587)                    n, $crate::BitFlags::CONST_TOKEN) }
[588](https://docs.rs#588)        }
[589](https://docs.rs#589)    };
[590](https://docs.rs#590)}

[613](https://docs.rs#613)
[614](https://docs.rs#614)impl<T> BitFlags<T>
[615](https://docs.rs#615)where
[616](https://docs.rs#616)    T: BitFlag,
[617](https://docs.rs#617){
[618](https://docs.rs#618)    /// Create a `BitFlags` if the raw value provided does not contain
[619](https://docs.rs#619)    /// any illegal flags.
[620](https://docs.rs#620)    ///
[621](https://docs.rs#621)    /// See also: [a convenience re-export in the `BitFlag` trait][BitFlag::from_bits],
[622](https://docs.rs#622)    /// which can help avoid the need for type hints.
[623](https://docs.rs#623)    ///
[624](https://docs.rs#624)    /// ```
[625](https://docs.rs#625)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[626](https://docs.rs#626)    /// #[bitflags]
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[628](https://docs.rs#628)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
[629](https://docs.rs#629)    /// enum MyFlag {
[630](https://docs.rs#630)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[631](https://docs.rs#631)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[632](https://docs.rs#632)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[633](https://docs.rs#633)    /// }
[634](https://docs.rs#634)    ///
[635](https://docs.rs#635)    /// let flags: BitFlags<MyFlag> = BitFlags::from_bits(0b11).unwrap();
[636](https://docs.rs#636)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[637](https://docs.rs#637)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[638](https://docs.rs#638)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    /// let invalid = BitFlags::<MyFlag>::from_bits(1 << 3);
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    /// assert!(invalid.is_err());
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    /// ```
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    #[inline]
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    pub fn from_bits(bits: T::Numeric) -> Result<Self, FromBitsError<T>> {
[644](https://docs.rs#644)        let flags = Self::from_bits_truncate(bits);
[645](https://docs.rs#645)        if flags.bits() == bits {
[646](https://docs.rs#646)            Ok(flags)
[647](https://docs.rs#647)        } else {
[648](https://docs.rs#648)            Err(FromBitsError {
[649](https://docs.rs#649)                flags,
[650](https://docs.rs#650)                invalid: bits & !flags.bits(),
[651](https://docs.rs#651)            })
[652](https://docs.rs#652)        }
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    }
[654](https://docs.rs#654)
[655](https://docs.rs#655)    /// Create a `BitFlags` from an underlying bitwise value. If any
[656](https://docs.rs#656)    /// invalid bits are set, ignore them.
[657](https://docs.rs#657)    ///
[658](https://docs.rs#658)    /// See also: [a convenience re-export in the `BitFlag` trait][BitFlag::from_bits_truncate],
[659](https://docs.rs#659)    /// which can help avoid the need for type hints.
[660](https://docs.rs#660)    ///
[661](https://docs.rs#661)    /// ```
[662](https://docs.rs#662)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[663](https://docs.rs#663)    /// #[bitflags]
[664](https://docs.rs#664)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[665](https://docs.rs#665)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[666](https://docs.rs#666)    /// enum MyFlag {
[667](https://docs.rs#667)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[668](https://docs.rs#668)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[669](https://docs.rs#669)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[670](https://docs.rs#670)    /// }
[671](https://docs.rs#671)    ///
[672](https://docs.rs#672)    /// let flags: BitFlags<MyFlag> = BitFlags::from_bits_truncate(0b1_1011);
[673](https://docs.rs#673)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[674](https://docs.rs#674)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[675](https://docs.rs#675)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[676](https://docs.rs#676)    /// ```
[677](https://docs.rs#677)    #[must_use]
[678](https://docs.rs#678)    #[inline(always)]
[679](https://docs.rs#679)    pub fn from_bits_truncate(bits: T::Numeric) -> Self {
[680](https://docs.rs#680)        // SAFETY: We're truncating out all the invalid bits, so the remaining
[681](https://docs.rs#681)        // ones must be valid.
[682](https://docs.rs#682)        unsafe { BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked(bits & T::ALL_BITS) }
[683](https://docs.rs#683)    }
[684](https://docs.rs#684)
[685](https://docs.rs#685)    /// Create a new BitFlags unsafely, without checking if the bits form
[686](https://docs.rs#686)    /// a valid bit pattern for the type.
[687](https://docs.rs#687)    ///
[688](https://docs.rs#688)    /// Consider using [`from_bits`][BitFlags::from_bits]
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    /// or [`from_bits_truncate`][BitFlags::from_bits_truncate] instead.
[690](https://docs.rs#690)    ///
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    /// # Safety
[692](https://docs.rs#692)    ///
[693](https://docs.rs#693)    /// All bits set in `val` must correspond to a value of the enum.
[694](https://docs.rs#694)    ///
[695](https://docs.rs#695)    /// # Example
[696](https://docs.rs#696)    ///
[697](https://docs.rs#697)    /// ```
[698](https://docs.rs#698)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[699](https://docs.rs#699)    /// #[bitflags]
[700](https://docs.rs#700)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[701](https://docs.rs#701)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[702](https://docs.rs#702)    /// enum MyFlag {
[703](https://docs.rs#703)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[704](https://docs.rs#704)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[705](https://docs.rs#705)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,
[706](https://docs.rs#706)    /// }
[707](https://docs.rs#707)    ///
[708](https://docs.rs#708)    /// let flags: BitFlags<MyFlag> = unsafe {
[709](https://docs.rs#709)    ///     BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked(0b011)
[710](https://docs.rs#710)    /// };
[711](https://docs.rs#711)    ///
[712](https://docs.rs#712)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
[713](https://docs.rs#713)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
[714](https://docs.rs#714)    /// assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
[715](https://docs.rs#715)    /// ```
[716](https://docs.rs#716)    #[must_use]
[717](https://docs.rs#717)    #[inline(always)]
[718](https://docs.rs#718)    pub unsafe fn from_bits_unchecked(val: T::Numeric) -> Self {
[719](https://docs.rs#719)        BitFlags {
[720](https://docs.rs#720)            val,
[721](https://docs.rs#721)            marker: PhantomData,
[722](https://docs.rs#722)        }
[723](https://docs.rs#723)    }
[724](https://docs.rs#724)
[725](https://docs.rs#725)    /// Turn a `T` into a `BitFlags<T>`. Also available as `flag.into()`.
[726](https://docs.rs#726)    #[must_use]
[727](https://docs.rs#727)    #[inline(always)]
[728](https://docs.rs#728)    pub fn from_flag(flag: T) -> Self {
[729](https://docs.rs#729)        // SAFETY: A value of the underlying enum is valid by definition.
[730](https://docs.rs#730)        unsafe { Self::from_bits_unchecked(flag.bits()) }
[731](https://docs.rs#731)    }
[732](https://docs.rs#732)
[733](https://docs.rs#733)    /// Create a `BitFlags` with no flags set (in other words, with a value of `0`).
[734](https://docs.rs#734)    ///
[735](https://docs.rs#735)    /// See also: [`BitFlag::empty`], a convenience reexport;
[736](https://docs.rs#736)    /// [`BitFlags::EMPTY`], the same functionality available
[737](https://docs.rs#737)    /// as a constant for `const fn` code.
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    ///
[739](https://docs.rs#739)    /// ```
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    /// # use enumflags2::{bitflags, BitFlags};
[741](https://docs.rs#741)    /// #[bitflags]
[742](https://docs.rs#742)    /// #[repr(u8)]
[743](https://docs.rs#743)    /// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    /// enum MyFlag {
[745](https://docs.rs#745)    ///     One = 1 << 0,
[746](https://docs.rs#746)    ///     Two = 1 << 1,
[747](https://docs.rs#747)    ///     Three = 1 << 2,

# make_bitflags in enumflags2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enumflags2/latest/target-redirect/enumflags2/macro.make_bitflags.html

```
macro_rules! make_bitflags {
    ( $enum:ident ::{ $($variant:ident)|* } ) => { ... };
    ( $enum:ident :: $variant:ident ) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

`make_bitflags!` provides a succint syntax for creating instances of
`BitFlags<T>`. Instead of repeating the name of your type for each flag
you want to add, try `make_bitflags!(Flags::{Foo | Bar})`.

```
let x = make_bitflags!(Test::{A | C});
assert_eq!(x, Test::A | Test::C);
// Also works in const contexts:
const X: BitFlags<Test> = make_bitflags!(Test::A);
```

# BitFlags in enumflags2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enumflags2/latest/target-redirect/enumflags2/struct.BitFlags.html

`pub struct BitFlags<T, N = <T as RawBitFlags>::Numeric> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Represents a set of flags of some type `T`.
`T` must have the `#[bitflags]` attribute applied.

A `BitFlags<T>` is as large as the `T` itself,
and stores one flag per bit.

[§](https://docs.rs#comparison-operators-partialord-and-ord)Comparison operators, `PartialOrd``Ord`

`PartialOrd``Ord`To make it possible to use `BitFlags` as the key of a
[`BTreeMap`][std::collections::BTreeMap], `BitFlags` implements
[ Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html). There is no meaningful total order for bitflags,
so the implementation simply compares the integer values of the bits.

Unfortunately, this means that comparing `BitFlags` with an operator
like `<=` will compile, and return values that are probably useless
and not what you expect. In particular, `<=` does *not* check whether
one value is a subset of the other. Use [ BitFlags::contains](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.contains) for that.

[§](https://docs.rs#customizing-default)Customizing `Default`

By default, creating an instance of `BitFlags<T>` with `Default` will result
in an empty set. If that’s undesirable, you may customize this:

```
#[bitflags(default = B | C)]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum MyFlag {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C = 0b0100,
    D = 0b1000,
}
assert_eq!(BitFlags::default(), MyFlag::B | MyFlag::C);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#memory-layout)Memory layout

`BitFlags<T>` is marked with the `#[repr(transparent)]` trait, meaning
it can be safely transmuted into the corresponding numeric type.

Usually, the same can be achieved by using [ BitFlags::bits](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.bits) in one
direction, and

[,](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits)

`BitFlags::from_bits`[, or](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits_truncate)

`BitFlags::from_bits_truncate`[in the other direction. However, transmuting might still be useful if, for example, you’re dealing with an entire array of](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits_unchecked)

`BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked``BitFlags`.When transmuting *into* a `BitFlags`, make sure that each set bit
corresponds to an existing flag
(cf. [ from_bits_unchecked](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits_unchecked)).

For example:

```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)] // <-- the repr determines the numeric type
#[derive(Copy, Clone)]
enum TransmuteMe {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
}
// NOTE: we use a small, self-contained function to handle the slice
// conversion to make sure the lifetimes are right.
fn transmute_slice<'a>(input: &'a [BitFlags<TransmuteMe>]) -> &'a [u8] {
    unsafe {
        slice::from_raw_parts(input.as_ptr() as *const u8, input.len())
    }
}
let many_flags = &[
    TransmuteMe::One.into(),
    TransmuteMe::One | TransmuteMe::Two,
];
let as_nums = transmute_slice(many_flags);
assert_eq!(as_nums, &[0b01, 0b11]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-notes)Implementation notes

You might expect this struct to be defined as

Ideally, that would be the case. However, because `const fn`s cannot
have trait bounds in current Rust, this would prevent us from providing
most `const fn` APIs. As a workaround, we define `BitFlags` with two
type parameters, with a default for the second one:

Manually providing a type for the `N` type parameter shouldn’t ever
be necessary.

The types substituted for `T` and `N` must always match, creating a
`BitFlags` value where that isn’t the case is only possible with
incorrect unsafe code.

Create a `BitFlags<T>` from an underlying bitwise value. If any
invalid bits are set, ignore them.

```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
const FLAGS: BitFlags<MyFlag> =
    BitFlags::<MyFlag>::from_bits_truncate_c(0b10101010, BitFlags::CONST_TOKEN);
assert_eq!(FLAGS, MyFlag::Two);
```
Bitwise OR — return value contains flag if either argument does.

Also available as `a | b`, but operator overloads are not usable
in `const fn`s at the moment.

Create a new BitFlags unsafely, without checking if the bits form a valid bit pattern for the type.

[instead.](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits_truncate)

`from_bits_truncate`[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

All bits set in `val` must correspond to a value of the enum.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
let flags: BitFlags<MyFlag> = unsafe {
    BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked(0b011)
};
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
```

[, the same functionality available as a constant for](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#associatedconstant.EMPTY)

#[bitflags]

    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,

#### pub fn [intersects](https://docs.rs#method.intersects)<B: [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[BitFlags](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html)<T>>>(self, other: B) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html)

Returns true if at least one flag is shared.

Returns true if all flags are contained.

Inserts if `cond` holds, else removes

```
#[bitflags]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Debug)]
#[repr(u8)]
enum MyFlag {
    A = 1 << 0,
    B = 1 << 1,
    C = 1 << 2,
}
let mut state = MyFlag::A | MyFlag::C;
state.set(MyFlag::A | MyFlag::B, false);
// Because the condition was false, both
// `A` and `B` are removed from the set
assert_eq!(state, MyFlag::C);
```

# ConstToken in enumflags2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enumflags2/latest/target-redirect/enumflags2/struct.ConstToken.html

`pub struct ConstToken<T, N>(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

Workaround for `const fn` limitations.

Some `const fn`s in this crate will need an instance of this type
for some type-level information usually provided by traits.

A token can be obtained from [ BitFlags::CONST_TOKEN](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#associatedconstant.CONST_TOKEN). The relevant types
should be readily inferred from context.

For an example of usage, see [ not_c](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.not_c).

# FromBitsError in enumflags2 - Rust

`pub struct FromBitsError<T: `[BitFlag](https://docs.rs/trait.BitFlag.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

The error struct used by [ BitFlags::from_bits](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits)
and the

[implementation for invalid values.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.TryFrom.html)

`TryFrom`Note that the implementation of [`std::error::Error`]
for this type is gated on the `std` feature flag.

```
#[bitflags]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
#[repr(u8)]
enum MyFlags {
    A = 0b0001,
    B = 0b0010,
    C = 0b0100,
    D = 0b1000,
}
let result: Result<BitFlags<MyFlags>, _> = 0b10101u8.try_into();
assert!(result.is_err());
let error = result.unwrap_err();
assert_eq!(error.truncate(), MyFlags::C | MyFlags::A);
assert_eq!(error.invalid_bits(), 0b10000);
```

A trait automatically implemented by `#[bitflags]` to make the enum
a valid type parameter for `BitFlags<T>`.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Create a `BitFlags` with no flags set (in other words, with a value of 0).

This is a convenience reexport of [ BitFlags::empty](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.empty). It can be called with

`MyFlag::empty()`, thus bypassing the need for type hints in some situations.```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
use enumflags2::BitFlag;
let empty = MyFlag::empty();
assert!(empty.is_empty());
assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::One), false);
assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::Two), false);
assert_eq!(empty.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
```
Create a `BitFlags` with all flags set.

This is a convenience reexport of [ BitFlags::all](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.all). It can be called with

`MyFlag::all()`, thus bypassing the need for type hints in some situations.```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
use enumflags2::BitFlag;
let all = MyFlag::all();
assert!(all.is_all());
assert_eq!(all.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
assert_eq!(all.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
assert_eq!(all.contains(MyFlag::Three), true);
```

Create a `BitFlags` if the raw value provided does not contain
any illegal flags.

This is a convenience reexport of [ BitFlags::from_bits](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits). It can be called
with

`MyFlag::from_bits(bits)`, thus bypassing the need for type hints in
some situations.```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
use enumflags2::BitFlag;
let flags = MyFlag::from_bits(0b11).unwrap();
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
let invalid = MyFlag::from_bits(1 << 3);
assert!(invalid.is_err());
```

Create a `BitFlags` from an underlying bitwise value. If any
invalid bits are set, ignore them.

This is a convenience reexport of [ BitFlags::from_bits_truncate](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits_truncate). It can be
called with

`MyFlag::from_bits_truncate(bits)`, thus bypassing the need for
type hints in some situations.```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
use enumflags2::BitFlag;
let flags = MyFlag::from_bits_truncate(0b1_1011);
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
```

#### unsafe fn [from_bits_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.from_bits_unchecked)(bits: Self::Numeric) -> [BitFlags](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html)<Self>

Create a `BitFlags` unsafely, without checking if the bits form
a valid bit pattern for the type.

Consider using [ from_bits](https://docs.rs/trait.BitFlag.html#method.from_bits)
or

[instead.](https://docs.rs/trait.BitFlag.html#method.from_bits_truncate)

`from_bits_truncate`[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

All bits set in `val` must correspond to a value of the enum.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This is a convenience reexport of [ BitFlags::from_bits_unchecked](https://docs.rs/struct.BitFlags.html#method.from_bits_unchecked). It can be
called with

`MyFlag::from_bits_unchecked(bits)`, thus bypassing the need for
type hints in some situations.```
#[bitflags]
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum MyFlag {
    One = 1 << 0,
    Two = 1 << 1,
    Three = 1 << 2,
}
use enumflags2::BitFlag;
let flags = unsafe {
    MyFlag::from_bits_unchecked(0b011)
};
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::One), true);
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Two), true);
assert_eq!(flags.contains(MyFlag::Three), false);
```

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`
